item.title: Al Letson challenged a conservative activist on voter fraud. He abruptly ended the interview.
item.author: bounce-mc.us1_388705.10708550-d186966748@mail194.suw241.rsgsv.net
item.content:encoded: Readers, this week, you’re in for two firsts: the show’s first full-length video episode and its first guest to angrily storm off mid-interview. While interviewing conservative activist J. Christian Adams, host Al Letson challenged his claims of widespread voter fraud in the US—a claim that’s been widely debunked. After 13 minutes of back and forth, Adams abruptly left the interview, a moment that you can see right here on our Instagram page. Don’t worry, this week’s episode isn’t 14 minutes long. national voting rights correspondent Ari Berman swooped in at the eleventh hour. We even got Berman’s take on Adams’ quick departure: “If he feels so confident in his numbers and arguments, why would he be so defensive from the very beginning to extremely basic and fair questions that you were asking? You weren’t asking him gotcha questions. You were asking him very basic questions to defend his assertions, and he immediately got so defensive. It reminded me of President Donald Trump storming off when Kristen Welker pushed him on the 2020 election." But this episode is so much more than Adams. In it, Letson and Berman take a serious look at Adams’ and the Trump administration’s claims of voter fraud, their lack of evidence, and how they’re using these claims to rig the upcoming midterm elections. Trust me, it’s an episode you won’t want to miss.

item.title: ‘Mail early’: Election officials urge people to get ballots in pronto amid Postal Service slowdowns
item.author: SRS0=WFyy=IA=bh1234.vbnewsletters.votebeat.org=bounces+misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
item.content:encoded: I think we need to restore the Voting Rights Act. The Supreme Court has said that we can't do it by simply going back to the old 1965 list. But it does explicitly say that it's not hostile to a new pre-clearance formula, and there are any number of ways that we can devise them. But before we do that, we have to confront the very hard truth that, without a robust Voting Rights Act, we are seeing immediate, significant, and meaningful burdens on minority voters that result as a direct effect of the erosion of this law. So, what that coverage formula looks like should be up to Congress, but it's going to take actions by Congress in order to get this done. Whether the Supreme Court then looks at a new coverage formula and accepts it as a reasonable remedy, I can't say. But I think the evidence that we present in this book shows that it really should.

item.title: I won’t let my legal briefs do the talking
item.author: 1axbipo1irgzb0g5p0jb9p2t006x8r6vwo6ztv@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Now is not the time to hide. It is the time to stand tall and speak out.That is the message I have delivered at a series of events over the past few weeks. I have spoken to diverse audiences of business leaders, lawyers, students and concerned citizens.At each event, I was warmly received. People praised my work as a lawyer and as a vocal opponent of Donald Trump’s efforts to subvert democracy.Yet when I called on the audience to act and speak out, I too often heard the usual concerns: “I am just one person.” “My friends are MAGA.” “My clients or customers won’t like it.”I recently sat down with Semafor for an interview about Democracy Docket. The host noted that most lawyers prefer to let their legal briefs do the talking. Why, he wanted to know, don’t I follow that same approach?My answer was the same one I gave my audience: it is too dangerous to stay silent.It is true that the future of free and fair elections is playing out in courthouses across the country. But it is not enough for lawyers to litigate. They have an obligation to speak publicly and plainly about these cases.This is not a new frustration for me. For years, I have watched Republican lawyers take center stage promoting election-denial conspiracy theories while those charged with defending democracy hide behind their legal filings.During the Biden presidency, this disagreement spilled into public view when some in the White House criticized me for “fighting on every possible front — filing a flurry of lawsuits and exerting public pressure through the media.”Since Trump’s return to power, those critics have largely gone quiet. Yet too few people are willing to take on Trump directly, without caveats or false equivalence.Meanwhile, I have redoubled my efforts. I have continued to litigate, arguing in federal and state courts, including before the U.S. Supreme Court last term.My law firm is currently litigating nearly 90 voting and election cases in 41 states. They include some of the most consequential cases for the future of democracy and free and fair elections. The firm is also preparing for what may come next: post-election litigation, recounts and election contests.Even so, I refuse to stop speaking out. I won’t simply let my legal filings do the talking.

item.title: A 5-Year-Old's Questions for Google Home
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: A father who is totally embracing modern technology discovers that Google Home had saved a year's worth of data, including his 5-year-old son's questions. He is charmed by his son's curiosity about the world, and appreciates the funny parts. Rowan's questions are adorable. On the other hand, it's a bit creepy to think that all these commands to an app are recorded for someone else to find, and for Google to analyze and market. My children came to me with incessant questions about the world throughout their childhoods, which I tried my best to answer, even if I had to look it up. As a result, they thought I was the repository of all the world's wisdom. They know better now, but I wouldn't trade that experience for all the chocolate. (via Laughing Squid)

item.title: The Biggest Ball of Twine
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: In 1989, Weird Al Yankovic included a song called "The Biggest Ball of Twine in Minnesota" on his album UHF – Original Motion Picture Soundtrack and Other Stuff. The song was not in the movie, and was never released as a single. But it referenced a real story. In 1950, Francis A. Johnson of Darwin, Minnesota, started collecting sisal twine from hay baling. He rolled it into a ball that became enormous, and made the papers. But then Frank Stoeber of Cawker City, Kansas, decided to give Johnson a run for his money, and the race to get into the Guinness Book of World Records was on. You might even call it a war. Drunk History gave Patton Oswalt all the Scotch whisky he could drink and had him tell the story of the world's biggest ball of twine. It features special appearances by Colin Hanks, Seth Green, Steve Agee, and Weird Al Yankovic. Oswalt kept up pretty well considering, until he was asked to give us the moral of the story. At least he tried. This video contains NSFW language.

item.title: Satudys 80s Jam: Cher – If I Could Turn Back Time
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: By the time Cher released “If I Could Turn Back Time” in 1989, she had already lived several careers in one lifetime. She had been a folk-pop star with Sonny Bono, a television personality, a movie actress, a disco singer, and a successful solo artist. But somehow, at 43 years old, Cher was about to have one of the biggest hits of her career.Released on her album , “If I Could Turn Back Time” became one of Cher’s signature songs and one of the most memorable power ballads of the late 1980s.The song was written by Diane Warren, who had become one of the era’s most successful songwriters. Warren specialized in enormous emotional pop songs, and “If I Could Turn Back Time” fit perfectly into that tradition. Its subject was simple: regret over a damaged relationship and the desperate wish to go back and fix what went wrong.Cher was an ideal singer for it.Her voice had always possessed a distinctive combination of strength and vulnerability. She didn’t need to oversell the emotion. The slightly husky quality of her voice made the song sound like it was coming from someone who had actually lived through the regrets she was singing about.The production, however, made it unmistakably 1989.Big drums, synthesizers, layered backing vocals, dramatic guitar, and an increasingly enormous arrangement transformed the song from a relatively straightforward ballad into a full-scale pop-rock production. Everything builds toward the chorus, where Cher’s vocal becomes the emotional center of the recording.Then came the music video.And that is where “If I Could Turn Back Time” became permanently attached to 1980s pop culture.The video was filmed aboard the USS and featured Cher performing for sailors. She wore a black, highly revealing outfit that became almost as famous as the song itself. The video generated controversy and received restrictions on some television outlets, but it also made Cher impossible to ignore.The outfit became an enduring piece of pop-culture history, while the video itself became one of the defining visual moments of late-1980s MTV.Ironically, all the attention surrounding the video could have overshadowed the song.“If I Could Turn Back Time” became a major international hit, reaching the top 10 in several countries and becoming one of Cher’s most recognizable recordings. In the United States, it reached number three on the Billboard Hot 100.The song also demonstrated something remarkable about Cher’s career: she wasn’t simply surviving into a new decade. She was successfully adapting to it.The 1980s had been full of musical reinvention. Artists who had been successful in earlier decades had to figure out how to compete in a world dominated by MTV, synthesizers, enormous productions, and increasingly image-conscious pop.Cher understood the assignment.By the end of the decade, she had transformed herself once again.What makes “If I Could Turn Back Time” endure isn’t simply its gigantic chorus or unforgettable music video. It’s the emotion at the heart of the song. Regret is universal. Everyone has something they wish they could redo, something they wish they had said differently, or some moment they wish they could revisit.Cher takes that very familiar feeling and turns it into a huge piece of late-1980s pop.And the fact that she was already a veteran performer when the song became a hit makes the achievement even more impressive.“If I Could Turn Back Time” wasn’t the beginning of Cher’s career.It was another reinvention.She had already been famous for decades, but in 1989 she managed to become something else again: an MTV-era pop superstar with one of the decade’s most recognizable songs and videos.The song may be about wanting to reverse the past.Cher, however, was doing the opposite.She was moving forward—and proving that she wasn’t anywhere near finished yet.

item.title: Deno is joining Cloudflare
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: The Deno team released the first version of celld back in August - their open source implementation of the Durable Objects pattern from Cloudflare Workers.Today, Cloudflare are acquiring Deno outright, with the goal of building on to "make workerd self-hosting a first-class supported way to build and run apps using the Workers programming model" (see the Cloudflare blog.)The bad news is that Deno itself will not be maintained by Cloudflare beyond the next year:We will support the Deno runtime for another year with monthly releases containing bug fixes and security updates. After that year we will end our development of the Deno runtime. Deno will remain open source, and we welcome others who want to continue its development.Deno (and Node.js) creator Ryan Dahl explained that decision in a comment on Hacker News:It's a joint decision and I agree with it. I'm most invested in its success and have put the most work into it - and I no longer think it's where I can do the most important work. There are some good ideas in Deno and it's well engineered - but it ultimately is not solving big problems. It has been sucked into the gravity well of node compatibility, which forces it to behave exactly as Node does. Why reimplement Node? It works. Marginal performance or UX or security benefits are not enough.I'm interested in building powerful new abstractions. celld has been working remarkably well, depending only on object storage for coordination and persistence. It is not just a slightly different API to interact with the file system or network - it's an entirely new model for server development.My favorite feature of Deno has long been the permissions system, where you can run a Deno script and specify exactly which files and folders it can read and write to, and which network hosts it can access.

item.title: Cotton Heaving as He Races toward November
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I need to start these kinds of posts by saying: No. I absolutely do not believe Tom Cotton will lose his reelection campaign. But even races that aren’t in contention can give you a read on the partisan climate. The Cotton campaign just released an internal poll showing him 11 points ahead of Democrat Hallie Shoffner — 50% to 39%. A Libertarian candidate has 4% support and 7% are undecided. That’s a solid lead. And a result any candidate would be happy with. Except when you remember that Trump won the state with 64% of the vote two years ago and Cotton won reelection with 67% of the vote in 2020. In 2022, John Boozman won with 66% of the vote. Cook appears to list Arkansas as an R+15 state. And they’d know. But in terms of actual election results, it certainly seems more like an R+30 state. In any case, the point is clear: This is a big level of underperformance in an extremely red state.

item.title: Name Shame
item.author: Ernie Smith
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.content:encoded: The concept of nominative antideterminism, or when your name goes against everything that you represent, whether intentionally or not. Cecil Fielder, sadly, wasn't a great fielder. If I lived my life in a nominatively deterministic way, I would be a Muppet blacksmith. But unfortunately, I live in the real world, and my lot in life has put me on newsletter-writing duty. So I don’t quite live up to my name. But lots of other folks don’t, either. Recently, though, I had a bit of a thought monster: What about people or things whose lives have more or less completely gone against what their names suggest they should? I’ve seen a couple of names for this, but I’m going with nominative antideterminism, the idea that not everyone needs to live up to the lot in life they’ve been given on the surface. And the guy that got me thinking about it? A famous baseball player who definitely did not live up to his last name—and his son arguably didn’t, either. Today’s Tedium ponders the oddness of nominative antideterminism, which I guess lazy people could just call “irony.” The estimated number of people in the U.S. with the last name “Smith,” well above the second-most-common last name, Johnson. That number is significantly more than the number of blacksmiths in the U.S., a number that is around 5,000 to 10,000 based on various historic estimates. Sorry to tell you this, in case you have yet to figure it out on your own: Not everyone named Smith is a blacksmith.Cecil Fielder doing what he does best: Hitting a home run.A designated-hitter dynasty: Were the Fielders good fielders? that the best baseball player I knew of was great at hitting home runs … and not much else.His name is Cecil Fielder, and he was basically the first player in more than a decade to hit 50 home runs in a single season, a mark that eventually opened the floodgates for years of home-run races (and yes, doping scandals). Fielder’s performance for the Detroit Tigers during the early 1990s was frequently in conversation for the AL MVP, getting close but never quite clinching it. Problem was, the Detroit Tigers weren’t a particularly good team back then, even if Fielder himself was an electric player.But Cecil Fielder, who was notably a fairly big guy for a baseball star, had a problem, and it’s one that is laid out cleanly on his Wikipedia page:Fielder also had a reputation as a below-average fielder, mostly caused by his poor speed and range.This, my friends, is a great example of nominative antideterminism. Often, we draw attention to people whose name more of less lived up to their lives.See that smile on his face? That’s the look of a man who never thought he would steal a base.But Fielder, who was always a better slugger than a runner (he infamously only stole two bases in his entire 13-year career), did not excel at the very thing his name suggested he would. This most assuredly explains why he was regularly used as a designated hitter.A surprising number of “Prince Fielder error” videos on YouTube, but to be fair, most of us would probably not love our errors getting shared with the world. Just ask a journalist whoo doezn’t kno how 2 spel.His also-successful son, Prince Fielder, had a somewhat better reputation as a fielder than Cecil did. But he also led the league in errors at his position more than once, hinting that he might have also only partly lived up to his name.Defensively, he recorded a .992 fielding percentage playing every inning at first base.That’s not quite as succinct as the “below-average fielder” phrasing on his dad’s page. Was Prince also a below-average fielder?I kind of felt bad sharing that video of Prince Fielder making an error, so here’s a video of him winning the Home Run Derby at the 2012 MLB All-Star Game.Comparing Cecil’s stats with Prince’s tells an interesting story. While Prince’s career ended prematurely due to a career-ending injury, he played more games than his father, in part because he was playing at an all-star level more or less immediately. (Cecil, on the other hand, spent years paying his dues, including a season in Japan, before his breakout 1990 season with the Tigers.)Even so, their career fielding percentages ended up fairly similar. Overall, Prince’s fielding percentage was a mere .001 better than his father’s, but setting aside Cecil’s moonlighting at other positions, each had a .992 fielding percentage at first base.While on the surface Cecil might be a worse fielder, neither were particularly great fielders. In fact, Prince’s range numbers were actually lower than Cecil’s—but as Cecil was more frequently a DH, especially later in his career, you could probably have a good debate over who’s the worse fielder.Hey Cecil, Prince: Nobody would be mad if you changed your family’s last name to “Slugger.”The Bittersweet tale of Neversink, New York, the town whose original location ironically became a reservoirThe town of Neversink, New York, up in the Catskills of New York state, is more than 100 miles away from New York City by driving distance, and about 75 as the crow flies. But the ongoing demands of NYC were enough to change its fortunes and ensure that the city would always come up in textbooks about irony.Throughout the state of New York, ongoing demands to help support the ever-massive needs of New York City led to common cases of eminent domain or condemnation of small towns to make room for reservoirs to support the needs of a massive city. For example, the town of Gilboa, which started as a settlement in 1760 and became an official town in 1848, was flooded in 1926 by the Schoharie Reservoir, a dam built on the Schoharie Creek. The portions of the town that are now literally underwater are called Old Gilboa.In 1931, a case that went to the Supreme Court essentially gave New York flexibility to divert water from the Delaware River and its tributaries to ensure the city had a strong, continuous water supply. From the summary of :The diversion from the tributaries of the amount proposed by New York will not materially affect the sanitary condition of the river, its industrial and agricultural uses, its use as a source of municipal water supply, or its shad fisheries. But it is necessary that the diversion should be curtailed and regulated, and be accompanied by sanitary treatment of sewage entering the stream in New York, in order to prevent injury to the use and reputation of the river for recreational purposes in New Jersey, and in order to avoid an increase of salinity in the lower river and in Delaware Bay which would injure the oyster industry there.The result put small riverside communities like Neversink on blast, allowing the state to more or less move or remove towns that would potentially get in the way of giant dams. In 1941, thanks to a judicially empowered Board of Water Supply, it was decided: The original location of Neversink was condemned, in favor of allowing the state to divert water from the Neversink River for a reservoir that would supply drinking water to one of the largest cities in the world.And yes, that meant Neversink’s original location, which also dated to the 18th century, was destined to sink. The situation was bittersweet in more ways than one: Quite literally, a neighboring town to Neversink was called Bittersweet, and it was overtaken by the reservoir, too. Unfortunately, it, along with three other communities flooded for nearby reservoir, did not survive the condemnation.(One of those communities was named Eureka, which is a completely different kind of nominative antideterminism.)It took many years for the relocation to actually happen, because reservoirs take a long time to build. (A whole World War began and ended in the time between initial proposals and completion.) Moves like these created major challenges for communities similar to Neversink, as noted by a 2016 story on the similarly to-be-sunk towns of Pepacton, Union Grove, Shavertown, and Arena:Reservoir construction had been underway for two years when a crowd of townspeople gathered at Shavertown’s general store in 1949. Every day the work inched closer to completion, and so did the time they would have to leave the idyllic village where their families had lived for generations. The city of New York would dole out compensation for their homes and relocation, but this was a small comfort to some, who didn’t even know when moving day would arrive.“We are pushing construction as fast as the weather and the good Lord will permit us,” Irving Hite, president of the Board of Water Supply told the . They hoped to finish the project by 1955 and promised not to “take a single acre of land until it is absolutely necessary.”Meanwhile, the villages lived on borrowed time; farmers hesitated to plant or expand their herds.Like those towns, Neversink sank, but it ultimately survived the condemnation by moving its residents to another location nearby. Bittersweet, sadly but fittingly, did not. (Bittersweet was a good example of nominative determinism.)In its place sits a reservoir that, on a good day, can hold up to 34.9 billion gallons of water, and (via a network of other reservoirs and the Delaware Aqueduct), eventually makes the long trip to New York City, where it ends up in fancy glass water bottles that people may or may not drink when they go to brunch.That’s the tale of Neversink’s nominatively antideterministic life. On the other hand, Neversink was once nominatively deterministic in a completely different way: It was a dry town for 80 years, including during the period when it was getting flooded and they probably could have used the alcohol. (A hotel that straddled the towns of Montela and Eureka had some, but after the floodings, it suddenly became hard to find.)When we’re born a thing is created, it’s given a name. We don’t have control over it usually, unless we choose a stage name like David Bowie, or Elton John.But sometimes it’s entirely possible for a stage name that you decided for yourself to become antideterministic. That brings us to the tale of Johnny Paycheck, which, while directly inspired by a boxer, suggests a person who knows how to make a few bucks here and there. (But to be clear, not Cash. Different guy entirely.)But Mr. Paycheck’s name—which he legally adopted in the mid-1960s—turned out to be ironic in more ways than one. First, his biggest hit was called “Take This Job and Shove It,” which is literally about a regular paycheck. Later in life, Paycheck, born Donald Eugene Lytle, faced a number of legal and financial troubles and eventually filed for bankruptcy after he failed to pay his taxes.Nobody has to live up to their name. But it’s fascinating when someone fails to live up to a name that they personally chose for themselves.

item.title: Mike Ditka, Forever Chicago
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: The relationship between sports and the place where those games are played is largely a matter of fans developing a strong but mostly manageable addiction to their own pheromones. Ritual and iconography matter more than the actual results when the results don't meet the need; the first two are stable and reliable in a way the third will never be. It has always been thus.And so Mike Ditka, whose death at age 86 was announced by his family Friday morning, was and remains still Chicago in ways that no other figure in any other city could manage. Ditka explained Chicago's view of itself from head to toe, vocal inflections to hand gestures, minor local biases to general worldview. Chicago is Ditka just as Ditka was Chicago, and that self-reverential truth will remain true even after he's gone.Ditka was quite literally the face of the Bears from the moment he left the University of Pittsburgh to seek his fortune in football 65 years ago. His helmet with the white single-bar facemask and his gashed-up face behind it was the image of choice in their 1963 championship, the one that interrupted the Decade of Lombardi. Ditka's contractual intransigence in the face of the team's iconic (and iconically vice-gripped) owner, George Halas, reinforced that status despite the six-year endgame in Philadelphia and then Dallas that completed his playing career. Even Ditka's Super Bowl championship with Dallas in 1971 felt a bit odd, in that Why is that Chicago guy celebrating next to Roger Staubach? kind of way. He sent himself into exile rather than take what Halas was offering, but Ditka never really left.

item.title: The Secret To Living 194 Years Is Being A Turtle
item.author: Sabrina Imbler
item.content:encoded: Geriatric Jonathan has made the news again, this time for having his genome sequenced. The Aldabra giant tortoise, who is estimated to be 194 years old, is the oldest known land animal on the planet. (The ocean, which teems with glass sponges thousands of years old and Greenland sharks that have been swimming for centuries, takes longevity to different extremes.) As such, it is understandable why scientists would want to sequence Jonathan's genome. He's lived a long freaking time.Yet many of the headlines heralding this new inquiry into Jonathan's venerable age, which was published in , have made me laugh with their implications that we may follow in Jonathan's closely spaced footsteps. Consider Reuters: "A 194-year-old tortoise, world's oldest land animal, may hold clues to longer life." Or take : "Has 194-year-old tortoise Jonathan taught us the secret to longer life?" What are the clues and secrets to Jonathan's extremely long life? Mainly there is one: Jonathan is a turtle.I can hardly blame these publications for this headline format; the blueprint was in the press releases issued by the University of Cambridge and Vanderbilt University, both of which framed Jonathan as potentially holding the secret to a long and healthy life, which he very well could! The headline in IFLScience—"We Finally Know How Jonathan The Tortoise, The World's Oldest Land Animal, Is Still Alive And Kicking At 194"—is easily answered the same way. Jonathan the tortoise is alive and kicking because he had the good luck to be born an Aldabra giant tortoise. Were Jonathan a human guy, he would not be alive.

item.title: Is This Weird Quiz Game the Toughest F1 Video Game Ever?
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: 3. Which team was the best in the 80’s?Statistically, it’s McLaren, but that’s not a correct answer. The correct answer is “Mc Laren.” 4. Who is the youngest champion of ever?The correct answer in 1993 was Emerson Fittipaldi, but his full name cannot be accepted because it contains too many characters for the computer. The game will not take “Fittipaldi,” “Emerson,” or “E Fittipaldi.” The answer must be “Fit.”The real quiz, it soon becomes clear, is not a test of one’s F1 knowledge, but figuring out what the game expects to hear.Berger is a former F1 driver, and the game is so weird and forgotten that it’s not even listed on his Wikipedia page — and it might not have been an official game at all. What listed on his Wikipedia page is the epic prank war he waged against teammate Ayrton Senna:In an Australian hotel room, Berger filled Senna’s bed with frogs. An infuriated Senna confronted Berger, who replied, “Did you find the snake?” Senna retaliated by putting strong-smelling French cheese in the air conditioning unit of Berger’s room.

item.title: What’s To Be Done With Jerry Dipoto?
item.author: Lucy Bloom
item.content:encoded: During a Sept. 28 press conference, Mariners president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto stated unprompted that if he had been fired following this season, it would have been justified. This is an extremely funny thing to say when you have not lost your job, especially when contextualized by your firings of five of your colleagues in the surrounding 48 hours, all of whom you hired. The difference between having your hypothetical firing rendered justifiable and having your walking papers actually handed to you is, uh, the whole dang thing.This is the sports executive equivalent of an implied admission of guilt issued directly after having gotten away with that shit. Like O.J., Dipoto will not elude fate forever; nobody with his job ever really does. I do find it sort of interesting to consider what he has actually done wrong. While most anyone paying attention to him likely agrees Dipoto has some real bozo moments, I think we may disagree on the specifics. Likewise, we might wish for a different hand at the helm, but for what reason? It's worth considering what, exactly, Jerry Dipoto has done wrong.The 2026 Seattle Mariners dramatically wretched and quivered their way to a third-place finish in a truly dogshit American League West, scoring the fewest runs they have in a full season since 2015. This year’s squad had some injuries and a bit of bad luck, but that isn’t actually much of an excuse. Those 2015 Mariners, who Dipoto took charge of at the end of the season, needed to give Logan Morrison 500 real major-league plate appearances and employ Dustin Ackley in a serious capacity to have an offense that shitty. Anyway, in the 11 years since, Dipoto saw his title bumped to President of Baseball Operations, and rewarded the M’s by winning eight playoff games, total. The day before Dipoto admitted his firing would be justified, the M’s announced that Dan Wilson would be relieved of his duties as on-field manager. The day , Wilson’s shitcanning was followed by that of his bench coach, Manny Acta, as well as his first base coach, hitting coach, and infield coach. The hitting was obviously quite bad, and the infield was even worse, owing significantly to JP Crawford’s valiant losing battle with the position of shortstop. There are a wonderful variety of advanced defensive metrics out there, with bitterly conflicting philosophies; Baseball Info Solutions has one, FanGraphs has one, and Statcast has two different ones. No matter which one you prefer, if you stack all the 2026 team defenses up against each other, you will find the Mariners DFL.

item.title: Buckle Up: The Final 3 Weeks of the Campaign Are Gonna Be Some Kind of UGLY
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: We’ve endured some very dark days in Trump II, but yesterday was particularly grim — and a possible taste of what’s to come between now and Election Day.Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth exuberantly announced that the holiday season execution by firing squad of former Army Major Nidal Malik Hasan for the Ft. Hood shooting will be live-streamed.In New York City, an ICE agent shot and wounded a Dominican national who was in his car with his 5-year-old child in the backseat.In a televised debate in the Michigan Senate race, GOP nominee Mike Rogers used Islamophobic smears to baselessly associate Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed with terrorism — after which President Trump called El-Sayed a “Terrorist Sympathizer” in a social media post.Somehow, the Michigan Senate debate was worse than the Georgia Senate debate, where GOP nominee Rep. Mike Collins has so many ties to neo-Nazis that it’s hard to keep count, prompting Sen. Jon Ossoff to scoff that Collins had “hired half the Third Reich” in his congressional office.Against that backdrop, the Trump DOJ is actively seeking to vindictively prosecute former Trump White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson for allegedly lying to Congress as the star witness in the Jan. 6 committee hearings.While the chaos of Trump II is often erratic and unpredictable, yesterday’s events are all tied to the upcoming election one way or the other. Even the ICE shooting came only two days after ICE increased its daily quota back to 3,000 arrests a day ahead of the midterms. The collective desperation of Trump and the GOP to avert a disastrous electoral defeat is likely to produce some even darker days over the next three and half weeks.The Persecution of Cassidy HutchinsonThe vindictive prosecution of Cassidy Hutchinson is being improbably spearheaded by the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division. It would normally have absolutely no role in pursuing this kind of case, but the division is led by the ambitious Harmeet Dhillon, who is eager to audition for a promotion.Dhillon’s team began presenting purported evidence against Hutchinson to a D.C. federal grand jury this week. While most of the reports cast it as investigation into whether Hutchison lied to Congress, the Washington Post, citing an unnamed source, suggests there maybe a twist: “[P]rosecutors have been exploring charging Hutchinson with a civil rights violation, potentially bringing a more unusual case than a simple charge of lying to Congress, one of the people familiar said.”In Other Vindictive Prosecution News …A federal judge has cleared the way for Kseniia Petrova to conduct discovery into whether she was the victim of vindictive prosecution by the Trump administration. Petrova is the Harvard researcher who was detained at Boston’s Logan International Airport in February 2025 and later charged with smuggling for bringing frog embryo samples into the country for her research.New Info on Kurt Olsen’s Failed PolygraphThe exact circumstances of the failed polygraph of Trump DOJ official Kurt Olsen keep dribbling out. The latest, from the New York Times (emphasis mine):It turned out he had failed a polygraph test about his contacts with foreigners, which imperiled his security clearance, according to two people familiar with the matter. Mr. Olsen said he complied with all requirements regarding foreign contacts and had not resigned over his clearance, but declined to say more.With everything else going on, the Kimberly Guilfoyle scandal is almost a welcome relief — a Molière comedy of the Trump era.The official responses to the Wall Street Journal blockbuster were quite unimpressive.Secretary of State Marco Rubio spewed a lot of bluster in refusing to answer any questions about his ambassador to Greece — but he also offered no defense of Kimberly Guilfoyle:Vice President JD Vance was similarly unenthusiastic about rushing to Guilfoyle’s defense:Bad News for Kim: Loose Cannon Is TalkingIf there’s one thing to know about the latest Guilfoyle scandal, it’s that her accuser doesn’t exactly fit the profile of the most reliable narrator. So the WSJ really had to bring the receipts, as it describes here.Making matters worse for her is that her accuser seems to love the spotlight and spent the day talking to damn near any TV news outlet that would listen.With so few Trump scandals truly breaking through into the broader cultural zeitgeist, Guilfoyle’s brazenness, shamelessness, and sloppiness have combined to potentially make her the rare exception.Have a Good Holiday WeekendSee you back here Tuesday.

item.title: Another Mountaineering Documentary That Asks: What Is Wrong With These People?
item.author: Rafaela Bassili
item.content:encoded: Having leisurely picked it up one day without expecting to be taken in, Jon Krakauer’s arrested me from the first page. “Among my five teammates who reached the top [of Mount Everest], four … perished in a rogue storm,” Krakauer writes. “By the time I’d descended to Base Camp nine climbers from four expeditions were dead, and three more lives would be lost before the month was out.” deaths seemed to me a Shakespearean number. But the more I read about mountaineering, the more I realized that there was nothing extraordinary, per se, about tragedy in the mountains. On Everest alone, as many as 10 people die on average every year, a number that keeps climbing as temperatures rise. Krakauer’s book is so affecting because he refuses to look at this fact with nonchalance.In that, Krakauer seems to be a bit of an outlier. Nonchalance is a common trait in adventurers whose impossible feats break through to the mainstream; consider Alex Honnold’s maddeningly blasé attitude toward his own chances in . For those of us who are fearful, this ability to repress or at least temper the fear of death is the root of our fascination with extreme sports athletes. Most depictions of their exploits ask an obvious question: ? But that’s a deceiving question, because the answer, at least as far as the psychologies on display are concerned, is equally obvious: When he was asked why he wanted to climb Mount Everest, George Mallory—the English mountaineer who was among the first to break trail on Everest, and who died on his third attempt to summit the mountain in 1924—famously replied: “Because it is there.” But the rest of his quote is just as telling a glimpse into the reasoning of the high-elevation climber. The urge, he said, is “a part, I suppose, of man’s desire to conquer the universe.”

The outcome in that game will go a long way toward pissing off one fan base while making the other completely insufferable—that is, if the hurricane permits the game to be played at all.If you're just in it for the hate, there's always Texas at Oklahoma, although OU has taken a profound backward step of late and Steve Sarkisian is his own bad time in your living room. Now that the games are winnowing themselves down to a few bangers per week, we have elected to be more selective with our viewing habits; yes, there is college football five nights per week until Halloween, but that doesn't mean we or you or anyone else should be consuming most of it. We'll still do it, mind you—the regular season starts at the end of November anyway, and games of little notice still have their charms. They just have a more difficult task making themselves seen amid all this inventory.

item.title: What Cornell says about universities’ MAGA complicity
item.content:encoded: In the wake of a national story of an alleged gang rape at the The whole debacle has refreshed interest in the previous big controversy of Kotikoff’s brief but eventful presidential tenure: Cornell’s $60 million settlement with Donald Trump’s administration, which was announced in November 2025. The agreement was widely lambasted as a capitulation to the White House’s all-out war on diversity, equity and inclusion programs. Not only did the university implicitly concede that programs meant to help women and minorities are discriminatory against white men, they agreed to hand over data on race in admissions to the Trump administration and impose anti-DEI materials, provided by the White House, on faculty and staff. After the settlement was announced, the American Association of University Professors said in a statement that the agreement would “threaten some of the most vulnerable students on campus and invite ongoing federal government supervision to reduce the diversity of Cornell’s student body.” In July, the organization published an extensive report comparing the administration’s war on DEI to the Red Scare of the 1950s and called on university leadership to resist the Trump administration’s efforts to destroy racial diversity and gender equity efforts on campus. As the AAUP report shows, Cornell was far from the only university to cave to Trump; the norm for colleges and universities was rapid compliance. Diversity offices were shut down. Progressive student protesters were bullied and punished. Title IX protections, including rules protecting students from sexual harassment and abuse, were scaled back. Anecdotes have spread from faculty and students about a new chill descending over college campuses — a fear of retaliation for acknowledging the ongoing realities of racism, sexism and homophobia on campuses and in larger society. The fallout from the Cornell assault accusations, however, suggests that it may have been more than fear that was compelling this swift bending of the knee by many universities to Trump. There is also a degree of complicity. Progressive reforms to make campuses more welcoming to women and minority students are often a hassle for university administrators, even those ideologically who are aligned with the left. It means conflicts with board members, donors and alumni with more conservative leanings. It means having to handle student complaints of harassment, discrimination and even sexual abuse that would be easier to sweep under the rug. It means having to confront institutions — like fraternities — that reinscribe racism and sexism but are often simultaneously protected by the most elite and wealthy people connected to the universities. Giving into the Trump administration on DEI means being able to revert to older, easier ways of doing things — even if it comes at the expense of student freedom and safety. It’s worth remembering that Jane Doe filed her complaint before Trump was president. Her case has all the hallmarks of an institution that tried to make her go away. Cornell police excluded relevant language — including the unambiguous phrase “I was raped” — from their report to the district attorney on Doe’s statement. Her lawyer claims that the university made her believe that the authorities were pursuing a criminal investigation, even though her case had already been closed. As Cornell philosophy professor Kate Manne noted in an essay for New York magazine, the university’s student code of conduct has a stricter definition of rape-by-intoxication than New York State’s, which would seem to cover the situation alleged here, where a woman is as high and drunk as Doe admits she was. And yet only five of the seven men accused were expelled from school, even as she was forced to drop out due to the subsequent stress and anxiety. If Cornell is guilty of abandoning Jane Doe, it has no reason to fear consequences from the federal government for failure to enforce Title IX protections against sexual abuse on campus.If Cornell is guilty of abandoning Jane Doe, it has no reason to fear consequences from the federal government for failure to enforce Title IX protections against sexual abuse on campus. As the New York Times reported this week, the Trump administration barely enforced the law during his first term. In his second term, enforcement is basically nonexistent. According to analysis by the Washington Post, Cornell’s track record is already alarming. From 2018 to 2024, there were 1,216 reports of sexual assault, domestic and dating violence, and stalking on campus. Only 51 people were ever found responsible, and of those, fewer than half faced serious consequences.Jane Doe reported her alleged rape a few days after Trump got elected. With that history in mind, Cornell police and administrators could have had every reason to believe there would be no federal repercussions if they failed to reach a just outcome in her case.Jane Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told CNN that his client “was not somebody who was a legacy [student], from a wealthy family” and “came from a small town.” Fraternities, in stark contrast, enjoy immense protections from exactly those wealthy people from legacy families. As historian Nick Syrett, author of “The Company He Keeps: A History of White College Fraternities,” told Time, former fraternity members are “a base of alumni that universities don’t want to upset because they’re generous and they’re powerful.” Whatever an administrator’s personal feelings, in a situation like this, it is objectively easier to cut loose an alleged victim rather than take on alleged assailants who are well-connected to powerful elites.From a purely self-interested point of view, the Trump administration’s demands that schools give up policies and programs to help women and minority students is a win-win for administrators. It allows school leaders to give up a miserable, uphill battle against elite forces, while handing them a way to deflect blame onto the White House for forcing them into it.We can’t peer into the hearts of administrators and know the exact mix of complicity and fear that drove these capitulations. But the Cornell case is a stark illustration of why the prospect of letting Trump have what he wants has a dark allure.

item.title: What kind of shithole country livestreams executions? Our kind.
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: For We the People, life continues to out of control.Basic goods and services remain unaffordable. Inflation and unemployment are on the rise. Our food is unsafe to eat. Our government lies to us. Our once-staunch allies hate our guts, and openly mock us. Masked, trigger-happy federal thugs roam the streets of our cities. Our hallowed national monuments have been shuttered, or bulldozed to rubble.Our detached, demented president has completely checked out of fixing any of this shit, preferring to focus on useless vanity projects in honor of his own crappy self.But We the People getting one very special thing, and it’s just for us. Know what that one thing is? Get ready for it: Public executions.Hegseth on Nidal Hasan: “He’s gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be. We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it. That it’s public. Because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”Seriously, what the damn?Did you notice how completely fucking excited Piss-Drunk Pete was, in that clip? He was absolutely as he burbled away at a mile a minute about how the military was going to publicly kill the shit out of someone. That’s insane. happy about meting out death — and nobody who’s that over-the-moon about killing should be put in charge of the lives of others.We’re going backwards as a country. The last public execution in the US was the hanging of some dude named Reiney Betha, on August 14, 1936. After that, states came to their senses, realized that kind of spectacle was barbaric, and stared passing laws against it.And now, Piss-Drunk Pete wants to bring it back, because he thinks that shit’s awesome. As always with these fuckfaces, Hey, you know what other country also does public executions? Iran. Isn’t Preznit Fuckwit always telling us how we’re more civilized than they are? That’s such a cute story, Donny, tell it again.Oh, but at the same time we’re going backwards, we’re also going forwards. We’re bringing public executions into the twenty-first century. Check out this abomination.The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said.A Defense Department official told the BBC the execution of Nidal Hasan, who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, would be livestreamed.It is believed it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. The decision to livestream it is “unprecedented in the modern era” and “on uncertain legal terrain,” said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.Oh, come on. Are you fucking me?! Who’s going to watch a livestream of someone getting firing-squadded to smithereens? Cultists? More importantly, who’s going to provide the livestream stream? Netflix? Amazon? Facebook? What corporation wants to be complicit in this barbarity? You’d hope the answer would be , but I can think of a few tech bros who would be that horny to curry favor with Dear Leader, and volunteer to host that shit for free.Is this who we want to be, as a nation? Do we really want to be known as the country that broadcasts state-sponsored death? Count me out. I want no part of this fuckery.It’s so much fun being a rogue nation, isn’t it?Ten days ago, the state of Tennessee tried to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection. If you’ve been following that story, you know that they fucked it up royally. Instead of dying, Pike spent hours moaning and crying in pain, and ended up in the hospital in a coma, with severe burns to her arms and shoulders.Imagine if that shit-show had been livestreamed.Maybe it should have been. Maybe the public outrage over that obscene level of cruelty would have started a national conversation about the death penalty.Now here’s something Dear Leader shat out onto his crappy app yesterday. It’s one of those posts that, when it shows up in your social feed, you go, ‘oh come on, that’s fake as fuck, not even Donny is crazypants’ — .The White House considers anyone that uses the term, “Artificial Intelligence,” as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, “Super Intelligence,” THE ENEMY! President DONALD J. TRUMPWho even talks like this? Just because we don’t agree on what to call the janky, six-fingered plagiarism robots, we’re now the all-caps ENEMY? How can any one person be that infantile?I’m so tired of him. I’m so tired of the relentless dumbfuckery. I’m so tired of the bone-crushing stupidity, and the childish if-you-don’t-agree-with-me-you’re-a-poopy-head mentality.And I’m fucking exhausted that there’s now an entire infrastructure devoted to making this utter failure feel good about his own shitty self.Did you know that Donny was awarded another Emotional Support Trophy yesterday?But Donny’s minders also did this: they took a genuine award that Donny’s uncle — the actual MIT professor, John G. Trump — had won in 1983, stuck it behind some chintzy gold frame, and with great fanfare, presented it to Donny, so that he could stand there, beaming, and pretend that he had somehow earned it all by his own Big Boy self.Look at this preening asshole. He’s just so eternally embarrassing. Put that shit down, numb-nuts, you haven’t won anything. And now, speaking of actual awards that Donny will win— “Thank you very much. If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”Really weird how there’s currently no Truth Social post from Donny, congratulating Navi Pillay for winning. What’s up with that?Well, it’s Friday, and — — we made it through another week in one piece. Let’s reward ourselves with some Daily Claudia and get out of here.Here are a couple more pics of Katie and her mom. These photos are undated but they’re obviously from the early 1990s.Have a great Friday, everyone. here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.content:encoded: The Not-So-Great Defector Bake Off, where Kelsey and Chris attempt to complete the technical challenges from the newest season of The Great British Bake Off in their own home kitchens, with the same time parameters as the professional-grade bakers competing on the show.When I was a child, there was nothing I loved more than preservatives. I loved soda. I loved fast food. I loved the kind of packaged treats that you get in a box at the grocery store, where each of them is individually wrapped in plastic, and the sugar content is so high that they make your teeth hurt. In particular, I loved Little Debbie's Nutty Buddies. The stacked wafers layered with chocolate and peanut butter called to me when my household had them. It was always a special treat. I can feel the crunch of the thin wafers between my teeth even now, probably 25 years since my last Nutty Buddy. I would eat one tomorrow. Such is the draw of childhood nostalgia and sweet treats.

item.title: Brazil’s Presidential Election Is One Piece Of A Larger, More Depressing Story
item.author: Patrick Redford
item.content:encoded: If one wanted to understand the alarming state of international politics in the Western Hemisphere through a single story, it'd be hard to beat Jose Antonio Kast visiting CECOT this past January.Kast spent nearly 20 years at the extreme right fringe of Chilean politics, mostly crusading against women's rights. His father was a Nazi, and not in any sort of metaphorical sense: He served as an Oberleutnant in the Wehrmacht in World War II. Various members of the Kast family also worked for the Pinochet dictatorship and have dedicated their lives to revanche. Last December, Kast won Chile's presidential election thanks in part to Donald Trump throwing his weight around, and before he took office, he went up to El Salvador to visit its notorious CECOT prison. Kast said he was interested in how to "import good ideas and proposals," such as the mass torture compound, in his quest to militarize Chile against the specter of narcoterrorists and illegal immigrants, and in doing so bring it into close collaboration with the Trump administration.This sort of thing has been happening all across Latin America since Trump strode back into power, with a rapidly dwindling handful of notable exceptions. The two most-populated countries cling to leftist rule, for now anyway. Claudia Sheinbaum's government is quite popular in Mexico and has managed to keep the U.S. relatively at bay, while Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is still in charge of Brazil. However, Lula underperformed in the first round of Brazilian elections this past Sunday, and Brazil is on the verge of electing Flavio Bolsonaro. The eldest son of the currently jailed and constantly leaking fascist former president assuming office of the second-most populous country in the Western Hemisphere would represent a total victory for the Trump-aligned right-wing movement in South America, and would by extension be a disaster for the country, the hemisphere, and the planet. How did we get here, and what tensions animate this broad coalition?

item.title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I've sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner.I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like:Start dev server and open in browserThis gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress.Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked.I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources.Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex:Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want it on the tag pages. I don't want it on the, um, blog index page. But I think I do want it to show up on the date-based pages. You know, if you navigate to September the 19th, and I sent a newsletter on that page, I think I want that to show up. So... this is- so I think we probably need a new model. The other thing is that I want them searchable, uh the Substack ones are not searchable, because those are actually just copies of other s- on content on my blog. These monthly ones do contain unique content, and spe- and once they're... published, like once they're made public a month after they've gone out, I want them to show up on my search results.Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build! You can read the full transcript, disfluencies and all, in this Gist.We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code.We got a surprisingly long way entirely by voice:A new model and migration to represent imported newsletters in Django, plus Django Admin configuration for thatFour working imports: The most recent Substack items via RSSEvery other Substack item via their undocumented API, which GPT-6 Astra knew about (it tried directly) and then ran a search to figure out how to paginate it and found this article by Karen SpinnerMy most recent private sponsors-only newsletter from a private repositoryNewsletters showing up on day and month archive pages too, but not on tag pages or my homepageWeekly Substack newsletters link to Substack; archived monthly newsletters have their own pagesIntegration with my site search engineIt was ready to ship. The catch was the imports: Astra offered to export data from my local copy so I could import that into production, but I wanted it to work like my other import scripts. Since some of the data lived in a private GitHub repository, this would involve creating a new API key, and for that I knew I'd have to sit at the keyboard for a while.Finishing it with a reviewOnce I had finished cooking and judged it mostly feature-complete, I had Codex create a branch and open a pull request.I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead.You can see the changes I made during the review in the extra commits on the PR. I fixed the import mechanism and made a few tweaks to the display of those public pages. It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR.The index page shows my most recent Substack weekly newsletters and GitHub sponsors monthly newsletters mixed together in reverse chronological order. Further down the page are links to my by-year archive pages.GPT-6 Astra designed the page, and then tweaked that design based on my vocal feedback from glancing at the local preview across the kitchen.Better for multi-tasking than as a daily driverOpenAI using voice-driven demos like this one for things like DevDay - and they do work well in that environment. I don't think this is going to be a daily driver for me though.I've written before about how much "work" I get done using ChatGPT voice mode on my phone while walking the dog - mostly research and brainstorming, but occasionally actual development work by having ChatGPT write and test out snippets of code.This feels different. The addition of the visual preview, plus being able to type or paste things in via the keyboard when I need to communicate something that doesn't work vocally, makes this a much more powerful way of interacting with a coding agent.I still switch back to typing once I get down to the details of things though. Being able to paste in examples and error messages, or directly highlight the code or feature that needs changing, remains more efficient than trying to describe it in words.I mainly work from home, which is good because there's no way I'd want to talk to my computer like this in a shared workspace!The killer feature for me is the ability to multi-task. I usually cook with a podcast or TikTok running; now I can actually build stuff instead.

item.title: Who will stop Trump now from seizing voting machines?
item.author: 1axb2a54qx7g67d6wvvnght97tmq66zafeh1ur@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Convicted criminal and former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters is pushing a scheme to give the Trump administration control over voting machines. In August, she called on the Department of War “to go in and demand to have these machines in their custody.”More recently, her lawyer, election denier Peter Ticktin, suggested that Peters’ plan was to “get control over the ballots as soon as the machine spits them through and then do a recount.” And on Oct. 5, according to Trump ally Ed Martin, Peters met with Trump in the Oval Office to discuss election security.We have been here before.In December 2020, a group of conspiracy theorists sat in the Oval Office arguing that Donald Trump should declare a national emergency and order the secretary of defense to “seize, collect, retain and analyze” voting machines, equipment and electronically stored election information.The motley crew of election deniers pushing this approach included attorney Sidney Powell, Trump’s former national security adviser Michael Flynn and former Overstock.com CEO Patrick Byrne. The day before the meeting, Flynn had suggested that the president could invoke martial law and use the military to “rerun” elections in swing states.More important than who advocated seizing voting equipment was who opposed it. The White House counsel, his deputy and the staff secretary all helped stop Trump from signing the order. So did Attorney General William Barr. Even Rudy Giuliani opposed using the military.Those guardrails no longer exist.

item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Wars have been fought for a lot of dumb reasons, but when political, religious, or ethnic tensions are inflamed, it only takes a spark to light a conflagration. In medieval Italy, all those tensions were sprung into war by a bucket. To be honest, the two regions were already fighting, but the bucket incident blew everything up, drawing thousands of fighters to their deaths in the battle of Zappolino. It was called the War of the Bucket. Be aware that the last minute of this video is an ad, so it's not as long as it seems. (via Digg)

item.title: ttok 1.0
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I released ttok 0.4, ran , piped a file into the new version... and realized that it was defaulting to the GPT-4 tokenizer when it should very clearly default to GPT-5/GPT-6 instead!I figured switching the default was a reasonable excuse to finally ship a 1.0.OpenAI haven't actually confirmed that GPT-6 uses the same tokenizer as the GPT-5 family yet - there's an angry issue about it - but I found this commit by William Liu which reports on an experiment he ran confirming that the tokenizers are likely the same:All seven GPT models (5.5, 5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna, 6 Astra/Sol/Luna) report 44,794 tokens and match each other on every one of the 31 fixtures. GPT-6 introduces no input-count change on this corpus.

The state is a battleground for fights over voter access.Just this week, Montana saw big wins for voters with disabilities and for direct democracy. But other groups, including student voters, still face significant access barriers.A federal appeals court declined to rehear Minnesota's defense of its law seeking to combat election misinformation, voter intimidation and harassment.The denial comes after a panel of appeals judges ordered the lower court to block enforcement of the law.The exchange, unearthed from government documents, comes after New Jersey Gov. item.title: Chasing a Plane Across the Moon
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: Over the course of 10 years, he took photos and videos of birds and statues silhouetted by the moon, but planes eluded him.I realized if I wanted to film this, I was going to have to try a different approach. It wasn’t just going to happen by accident. So in February of this year, taking advantage of being in London, I decided to go near one of the busiest airports in the world to maximize my odds as much as possible.But while we were on our way, I had second thoughts. I felt like it took the fun out of it. It didn’t make sense to force it that much either. So we got off. I’m not going to spoil the video, but the whole thing is just so lovely — a meditation on obsessions, journeys, and finding meaning in your life. (via virginia)

item.title: Oh Hey, More AI Stuff — Is This Our Reliable Narrator?
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: Yet another update on the running AI discussion.Here’s an interview Ezra Klein did with a guy named David Robinson. And that interview is about a piece Robinson, a member of the Open AI safety and safety documentation team, wrote in The Atlantic announcing his resignation from OpenAI — a decision and announcement he is self-aware enough to note has become something of a cliche. I found the interview interesting and edifying, largely on the front I mentioned earlier about finding reliable narrators.Robinson isn’t a data scientist or a programmer. His role at OpenAI was essentially being the conduit between the teams building the LLMs and the knowledgable and interested public, specifically the people who write the documentation — what does this model do, how does it work, what are the possible safety risks. As is usually the case in any highly technical space, the people doing the work aren’t going to be writers and they’re usually not going to speak a language outsiders can necessarily understand. So you have people who are close enough to the work and the workers to understand what is happening and also able to speak human so they can communicate it to everyone else. Robinson led the team that served in that role.

item.title: Is This Guy Who Uses AI To Run His Fantasy Football Team The Biggest Loser In The World?
item.author: Samer Kalaf
item.content:encoded: Why does anyone play fantasy football? This is not a trick question, although it's also not particularly difficult to answer. Perhaps they do it for money, or they enjoy football, or they want a shared activity to help stay in touch with friends or family. Whatever the reason, the fun is in picking your guys and managing your little team and hoping you win more often than you lose. Some people have a healthier relationship to this endeavor than others. Still, if none of it appeals to you, then you can always not do it.

item.title: Which is Better: Buying or Renting a Home?
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Is it better to rent a home or buy one? It all depends. The TED-Ed lesson compares two people who made different choices. The amounts of money thrown around here are scary, because I've never had that much. But it's all relative. I told my kids to buy a house once they've decided where they want to live for many years to come. Otherwise, rent until you are ready to settle down. Princess bought one, where her kids can make all the noise they want. Dr. Dolittle rents. She and her husband come to my house and cosplay as house owners, mowing my lawn and doing other maintenance. Personally, I get a lot of satisfaction out of owning my home, but I never had to sign a 30-year mortgage. That's really scary.

item.title: Action Alert: Speak Out Against Taxpayer-Funded Political Ads
item.author: bounce_75b4552d-49c3-f111-bf5b-000d3a4fbe83_prod@bounce.myngp.com
item.content:encoded: This administration’s “flood the zone” strategy continues with actions that raise serious concerns about constitutional principles and the rule of law. As disheartening as these actions can be, we must meet them with informed engagement and expectations for a better future.Today, we are issuing our latest Action Alert, asking the public to speak out against the misuse of federal resources for partisan political promotion. The administration recently spent nearly $12 million in taxpayer funds on television ads promoting the President, with millions more allocated under a $20 million contract for additional ads selected to run during major broadcasts in the critical weeks before the midterm elections. Following widespread criticism, the President announced that the remaining ads would be paid for via his MAGA Inc. Super PAC.Both approaches raise serious questions under federal law, including restrictions on the use of appropriated funds for unauthorized publicity or political propaganda, the Hatch Act, and federal campaign finance laws. Shifting the payment method from taxpayer funding to privately raised Super PAC funds does not eliminate the need to comply with applicable legal restrictions. Our Action Alert outlines four steps you can take today. LDAD is grateful to our many volunteers who continue to help document important developments, raise concerns, and defend the rule of law. They do this in a variety of ways, for example:LDAD volunteer, Professor Mark Gordon, recently moderated an important election-related program co-sponsored by the Minnesota State Bar Association and LDAD entitled: Rules and Procedures for Voting in the Midterm Elections in MN.Lawyers Defending American DemocracyP.S. Thank you for your ongoing support of LDAD. Please help us protect the rule of law and the freedoms we hold dear by volunteering for our Meeting the Moment initiative and donating to our work.

item.title: A Novel About California’s Pluckiest Virgin Is Getting A Second Chance
item.author: Meghan Racklin
item.content:encoded: Names, the heroine of Cynthia Buchanan’s 1972 debut novel, , thinks to herself, “are so vital.” And with a name like Fortune, you’d have to try your luck in California. Although she prefers Fortunée: She calls this a “higher-type pronunciation,” though this also marks it as a maiden name. She’s never gotten lucky. At 30, Fortune is still a virgin, “and her virginity had burrowed in.” “Would life forget about her?” runs her inner monologue. “Overlook her? Pass her by? Misdial? Anxiety became a lifestyle.” Perhaps, as Fortune later comes to believe, names are “not all they’re cracked up to be.”In the tour de force of an opening chapter, Fortune emerges as a postmodern pastiche of a girl; we know little about her background, other than that she’s poorly educated, from somewhere in the South, and has a brother and a small handful of romantic disappointments whose impact she tries to suppress. She’s papered over the void of her virginity and her background like a teenager decorating a bedroom wall. She is a woman putting herself together from the spare parts of mass culture, a collage of magazine clippings, ’50s movie stars, and dating how-to guides, trying to form herself into someone a man might want—and the book itself is composed of, among other things, an advertisement for a dating service, a reality show audition transcript, court documents, and personal ads. It’s an allegory for America, its manufactured, impossible dreams, its naivete and excess, its delusional self-mythologizing. On publication, the grouped with Sylvia Plath's and Joan Didion's , calling the three "a natural trilogy," and going so far as to suggest that might be "the best of the three." The novel’s precise, timestamped detail may explain why it faded from view while and became modern classics (though all three feature some attitudes and language that now reads as offensively outdated). But ’s specific concerns are also what make it feel, if not exactly timely, like a premonition or a warning. “Language,” for instance, “haunted [Fortune]. The advertised word … the ‘you’ in advertising, the impossible ‘you’ spoke to her.” Fortune is, like many a chick-lit heroine, constantly in search of a job and a boyfriend, but Buchanan is keenly aware of the lonely logic of commodification that links her two pursuits. Now being reissued by Hagfish and read in a contemporary context, looks just as much like a funhouse mirror for our own times as it is an artifact of its own, presaging the dating apps, the endless scroll, the conspicuous consumption and pastiched personalities of our era, as it does a reflection of its own.

item.title: Everything We Know And Don’t Know About The Possible Plague Death At The Anti-Plague Institute
item.author: Sabrina Imbler
item.content:encoded: You might have heard by now of the scientist in Russia, 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, who died on Oct. 2 of an unknown illness. Shipilova worked in a lab at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, an institution founded in the 1930s to control and prevent—you guessed it—plagues. Russian health authorities have since quarantined the hospital where Shipilova died, along with staff at the institute and anyone else who came in contact with her. These are the facts.And then there are the murkier details, as well as the rumors. Shipilova was diagnosed with a pneumonia of unknown origin, per Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian public health agency. A governor of a neighboring republic said Shipilova died "possibly from the plague," and a Russian journalist wrote on his Telegram that Shipilova had broken a test tube before she got sick, reported There are reports of a second worker at the institute who contracted pneumonia, per the AP, and reports that several hospitals have been placed under quarantine, per NPR. Although the Russian government announced that "test results showed no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens in any of the contacts," the head of Rospotrebnadzor traveled to Irkutsk to meet with the regional anti-epidemic commission, CNN reported. The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, meanwhile, has not responded to journalists' questions.Many of journalist's questions—such as "Is there a plague happening in Russia?" and "Should I be freaking out?"—don't have clear answers. But before your mind fills with images of eerily avian plague doctors, these are the questions we can answer, at least for now.

item.title: A Blue Wave Won’t Mean Shit If The Chumps Get Their Way
item.author: Drew Magary
item.content:encoded: Drew Magary’s Thursday Afternoon NFL Dick Joke Jamboroo runs every Thursday at Defector during the NFL season. Got something you wanna contribute? . You can also read Drew over at You might have heard there’s an election coming soon. Given that this is The Most Important Election Of Our Lifetimes, No. 536, the campaign industrial complex has rested a 1,000-pound boulder atop the SPAM button in an attempt to curry favor with you, the voter. This is why I, a Marylander, am bombarded with campaign ads/flyers/robocalls 48 hours a day, including TV ads for Senate candidates in states nowhere near mine, Ohio and Texas in particular. It’s also why Donald Trump has used taxpayer money to buy up national airtime for an ad that features him walking menacingly toward the camera, like you’re about to be his next victim. Thank you, Mister President!You’ll notice that much of this long-distance haranguing is being waged by the Republican Party, almost certainly because their current polling nationwide is abysmal. If those numbers hold—although you and I know better than to trust polls—the GOP stands on the brink of losing both houses of Congress, plus a number of crucial state elections. That’s why they’re flooding the airwaves with a steady stream of dogshit. These are tactics of desperation.
