item.title: I tried to move my notes out of Emacs. I failed. Again.
item.author: Jack Baty
item.content:encoded: Every so often I suffer from what I call "Emacs Fatigue". It's closely related to "Text File Fatigue". Using Emacs tends to pull one toward using it for everything, which is what I'd done. Then, I simply grow tired of staring at the same thing every day. When this happens, I "decide" to uproot my life and move my notes into something else. This time, that something else was Bear.Bear is great. It's solid, beautiful, and refreshingly simple. It syncs flawlessly (for free) and runs on macOS and iOS. It's also inexpensive. It uses an SQLite database, which doesn't bother me. Databases are great at this stuff. All the "But but what if the database...?!" talk is mostly hearsay anyway.The thing that made me twitchy was that it felt like my notes were "in there". It's not the database. It's the fact that everything is in an app, and that app makes me need to use that app. This is how I'd started to feel about Emacs, but mostly due to Org mode.Bear is macOS and iOS only, which should be fine for someone like me who has "decided" to live on macOS. And yet, Linux continues to emit a low-grade hum in the back of my head that I can't ignore.If I don't want my notes in Org mode files, but I'm still drawn toward Emacs, what should I do? Denote! That's where they'd all started in the first place, but as .org not .md. I'd nearly forgotten that Denote handles Markdown files natively. One Emacs configuration change and I was back where I belong. And since Bear notes are already Markdown, all it took was an export and a (Claude Code-assisted) conversion script for file names, links, and attachments.So yes, I've done that thing where I quit using Emacs only to come crawling back later. I know better, but knowing better doesn't stop me. Maybe I'll work on a sync/bridge between Denote and Bear. That would be neat.

item.title: Dylan Larkin And The Red Wings Are Having Agonizing Breakup Sex On Live TV
item.author: Lauren Theisen
item.content:encoded: Dylan Larkin is still a Red Wing, even though he doesn't want to be. His offseason trade request, arriving after 11 seasons with the club and a mere five playoff games (all as a rookie), symbolized the franchise's inability to shift out of neutral and forced fans to stare the worst-case scenario in the face: After all these years of waiting, maybe the Wings remain closer to the No. 1 draft pick than a playoff run. As the team's second-best goal-scorer and top-line center, Larkin would be impossible to replace quickly, so him deciding that he's given up on this project and would rather just get to the postseason with a contender, now that he's in his 30s, is a frustrating setback.It's an issue, too, that has yet to be resolved as the Red Wings wrap their first week of regular-season play. The list of teams that Larkin is reportedly willing to waive his no-movement clause for is tiny and elite (not to mention cap-crunched), and Detroit, which doesn't even have a non-interim GM at the moment, has yet to swing a deal. Consequently, Larkin was stripped of his team captaincy, and he got lustily booed by fans when his name was announced on opening night. He sat out the first two losses of the season with injury, while the Wings allowed five goals over four-and-a-half periods before they even got on the board. And when he returned to the ice in front of a sad-looking turnout Tuesday night against Ottawa, those who chose to voice their opinion were generally not happy to see him.But this game played out differently than the Wings' previous poor showings. While Ottawa got the first goal not even three minutes in, the men in red mounted a meaningful response, scoring four straight en route to a 5-3 win. And it was Larkin who played the biggest role of anyone—not as a pariah, but as a talented forward who has consistently injected at least a little bit of light into otherwise dark passages.

item.title: The TV People Are Talking About Deshaun Watson All Wrong
item.author: Drew Magary
item.content:encoded: If you missed last week’s tilt between the Steelers and Browns, don’t grieve. The game itself was inessential, and Amazon Prime’s coverage of the game all but incentivized the audience to do anything else with its evening. That’s because Amazon’s broadcast team decided to treat Browns QB Deshaun Watson, a proven and unrepentant menace to women, with the kind of soft-focus treatment usually reserved for diabetic Olympians. Watson was feted in the pregame show, during the main telecast, and even in the postgame. Under normal circumstances, this coverage would have been vile. In the wake of a Cornell rape scandal that has become national news, it’s somehow even more galling. There’s a way to talk about Watson, and the 3-1 Browns, without stooping lower than hell’s seventh circle. So Arif Hasan and I endeavored to do just that on this week’s episode of . https://art19.com/shows/the-distraction/episodes/dda3686b-7abc-4abe-8719-7953d6f9860a Thankfully, there’s more. As our newborn show continues its steady development into becoming an elite podcast, we have tweaked the format of by every game, throwgasm-style, instead of blithely picking it. We also made sure to carve out ample time to make fun of the strugggggling Eagles, talk up the surprisingly awesome Jaguars, and attempt to make sense of the undefeated but offense-less Vikings. All of that was WAYYYYY more fun to talk about than Deshaun Watson, lemme tell ya.

item.title: Desperate GOP Scrambles to Defend Once-Solid Red Seats
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: Republican political consultants are practically falling over each other to make the most dire pronouncements about the GOP’s fate in the midterms.“If the bottom continues falling out like it has been, this will be worse than 2006,” one national Republican strategist tells Politico. Democrats picked up 31 seats that year and ended 12 years of GOP control of the House.I’m deeply skeptical of poll-driven narratives in election coverage — which the past few cycles have only reinforced — but there’s quite a bit more to go on than just public opinion surveys in assessing the state of the midterms. Between now and Election Day, I’ll be frequently including in Morning Memo a sampling of those additional data points: which races are being newly contested and which aren’t, where the spending is going and where it’s not, and other markers on the state of the race — including President Trump’s unscripted intemperate outbursts.The Cook Political Report on Tuesday moved three Senate races in Democrats’ favor:Kansas from Lean Republican to Toss UpNorth Carolina from Lean Democrat to Likely DemocratNew Hampshire from Toss Up to Lean DemocratIn deep-red South Carolina, appointed Sen. Darline Graham (R) is struggling to hold on to her late brother’s seat, forcing the Senate Leadership Fund to dump $5 million into her race against Dr. Annie Andrews. In a sign of the brewing trouble for the GOP, Trump went on a “crazed, manic tirade” this week against Andrews, using an anti-trans slur among other attacks.On the House side, in a sign of increasing desperation, Republicans have quietly resumed backing Rep. Max Miller (R-OH) despite earlier calls from within the party for him to drop out of the race amidst allegations against him of domestic abuse.Election Ratfuckery AlertThe Trump administration continues to pull levers and push buttons to try to abuse the power of the federal government to swing the election its way:The Department of Homeland Security has investigated more than 150 voter registration groups in search of evidence that they’re helping noncitizens illegally register to vote, according to internal documents obtained via FOIA and provided to the New York Times. The DHS effort has been most heavily focused on groups in New Jersey and Pennsylvania. DHS has considered using undercover agents in its investigations, the documents reveal. Also of note:The documents also reveal that Heather Honey, a prominent 2020 election denier who now serves as the department’s point person on “election integrity,” provided 48.4 million records of unknown provenance to federal investigators who are trying to find noncitizens on the voter rolls.The Trump DOJ dispatched federal prosecutors and an FBI agent to monitor polls in Maricopa and Pima counties in Arizona during its July primary election — a dramatic departure from past DOJ practice of using Civil Rights Division personnel as poll monitors to avoid intimidating voters and local election officials, Democracy Docket reports. The Trump DOJ is apparently planning to continue using prosecutors as poll monitors in the general election, telling Democracy Docket that “department attorneys, including prosecutors, will serve as election monitors.”In the run-up to election, ICE has begun asking detainees if they have ever voted illegally and, if so, whether in person or by mail, the WaPo reports. “ICE reviews credible allegations of potential criminal activity within its jurisdiction, including allegations related to election integrity,” an ICE spokesperson told the newspaper.The Big Lie Crazies Still Big Lie-ingBig Lie purveyor Tina Peters met with President Trump in the Oval Office this week to discuss “election integrity.” Meanwhile, election denier Cleta Mitchell is “pushing a scheme to have Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick seize voting machines,” Democracy Docket reports. Former Trump DOJ official Ed Martin helpfully ties all of this together:: All of this comes as the Trump DOJ continues to fight to enforce a grand jury subpoena of Fulton County, Georgia, for the names and personal information of the hundreds of staffers, contractors, and volunteers who worked on the 2020 election. Jan. 6 never ends.How Trump Can Still Subvert the ElectionElection law expert Rick Hasen gives a fairly glowing assessment of how well the guardrails have held so far against Trump’s assault on free and fair midterm elections — and assesses where the greatest risks remain.Another Classic Trump ConTrump’s claim that he and his super PAC will start paying for the pro-Trump TV ads that the taxpayer funds have been used to air during the stretch run of the midterms that he will reimburse the government for the expenses it already incurred.“White House officials clarified on Tuesday to Politico that the president’s post did not mean the PAC would pay for the spots that had already aired,” Politico reports.More than $10 million of a $20 million DHS contract has already been spent on the ads, the NYT calculates.: Last year, when he was acting deputy attorney general, Emil Bove pressed the FBI to illegally investigate ICE protesters in Los Angeles in violation of their constitutional rights and bureau policy, an FBI whistleblower alleges. The allegations emerged in a whistleblower complaint to leaders of the Senate Judiciary Committee by Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s LA field office. Fields also claims that FBI Director Kash Patel succumbed to pressure from the White House to investigate another group of ICE protesters after President Trump saw them in TikTok post.: After purging career lawyers, the Trump DOJ’s once-prestigous Civil Rights Division — led by Trump loyalist Harmeet Dhillon — is turning to partisans and conspiracists to fill its depleted ranks, the NYT reports.: Lawyers for David Hearn, the man wrongly accused of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool, sent a letter to the inspectors general of DOJ and DOI asking for an investigation of the circumstances of his arrest and subsequently dismissed prosecution. Among his lawyers is Michael R. Bromwich, a former DOJ IG.EU Preps for Mass Casualty Russian AttackIn a restricted, closed-door meeting last Wednesday, EU ambassadors discussed how to respond collectively to a hybrid Russian attack that results in mass casualties, a risk they fear looks increasingly likely, Politico reports.“[W]hen a majority of the justices on our highest court show themselves to be consistently indifferent to the growing chasm between law and justice, it is not ‘public rhetoric’ that causes Americans to distrust the Court. It is the Court that surrenders its own legitimacy in the eyes of the public.”—

item.title: ‘Content Machines’ Asks The Right Questions About Publishing In The Platform Era
item.author: Madeline Lane-McKinley
item.content:encoded: Every season, there’s a particular sort of novel that elicits its own genre of disdain. It’s somehow “too personal” and also lacking in “depth.” It’s called things like indulgent, trashy, lazy, artless, frivolous, embarrassing, or perhaps just very online. This is the of our times, the gimmick of the not-quite-memoir, autofiction. Over the summer, as Rachel Cusk’s took its turn, Grace Byron remarked that by now, speculation over the genre’s boundaries of fact and fiction is “its own bloodsport.” Since its rise in the 2010s, “the only thing trendier and triter than writing autofiction is hating autofiction,” as Sanjena Sathian put it in 2022. But why, if it so silly and unserious, does this genre seem to pose such an enduring threat?To perennial debates over autofiction and much else, Sarah Brouillette’s latest book is a welcome redirection from questions of literary merit to a sharp historical analysis of the contemporary publishing industry—and many of its attendant anxieties. Brouillette, a literary scholar and Marxist-feminist whose cultural criticism has appeared in Defector, continues the interventionary work of her previous books on UNESCO, the creative economy, and the global literary marketplace, regarding contemporary questions about the “fate of the literary”: "We are told to worry about the threats to literary art’s essential moral seriousness, distinction, difficulty, and purpose," as she writes in . "We are warned that publishing today is overrun with what are basically entitled consumers: ideologically inflexible, uncomfortable with hard ideas and disagreement, untrained, incapable of nuanced thought, and always on the edge of tears or outage." Rather than stoking the panic, historically situates it, uncovering urgent political questions about an era of publishing permeated by digital platforms such as Wattpad, Kindle, and Audible, and social media phenomena like BookTok and Bookstagram. examines digital platforms as “technologies of precarity,” instrumental to the ever-worsening labor conditions in publishing. More specifically, Brouillette conceives of platforms as forces of feminization. It’s not just that women are doing more of the jobs and that the jobs are getting worse. Women are doing more of these jobs precisely because they are worse. “The more work in writing and publishing becomes available only to those willing to do it on a contingent basis,” as Brouillette explains, “the more it is likely to be women doing it,” as workers accustomed “to low-prestige work and to taking jobs that allow them to continue with housework and childcare.” This is the case across many workforces, and what we’re always really talking about whenever masculinity is in “crisis.”

item.title: Padres-Brewers Has Been The Best Of October Baseball
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: The single discordant note in the otherwise effervescent National League Divisional Series between the Milwaukee Brewers and San Diego Padres so far was a brief shot of new Padres owners Jose E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones watching Game 3. It was easy to imagine them, less than two months into the new gig, assuming that it would always be like this. All they know is winning two out of every three games, playing before sold-out houses, and learning cool inside-baseball phrases like "Goddammit, Merrill." They'll find out soon that this sort of thing is too good to last.This series has not only been the best of the eight played so far in this postseason, but the best in years. Two indisputably accomplished teams, each with very different approaches and without the burdens of franchise legacy, have played taut and delightful baseball replete with stuff like speed, athletic defense, rapid-response scoring, bold tactical choices, and pitching being tested but only occasionally bested. It's the stuff that makes watching your $3.9 billion investment action worth the bother of coming to the park. All that, and "Goddammit, Merrill" too.The Padres extended the series at least a day with an incandescent 4-3 win Tuesday night, and they now trail the Brewers, the best team in the game during the regular season, 2-1 in a not-enough-games-no-matter-who-wins series. All three games have been decided by one run and hung precariously in the balance to the end. That was most thrilling in Game 2, when Brewers outfielder Jackson Chourio's walk-off hit in the gap scored two runs and stole the result from the Padres and their overpowering Padres closer Mason Miller. Because some ethereal things are happening here, Chourio opened Game 3 with a similar drive, only to have it seized before it landed by a diving San Diego center fielder Jackson Merrill, the name behind the curse.

item.title: Anti-Patterns in Software Blogging
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Some excellent writing advice from Michael Lynch. Michael warns against "meandering intros", misjudging your reader's existing knowledge, assuming they'll read your previous posts, and excessive formality.He also warns against overreliance on links as an excuse not to explain terminology. This one hurt! I do this all the time, but I have a nagging suspicion that almost nobody ever clicks on them.(In a Lobste.rs comment Michael clarifies that "My rule of thumb is that my article should still make sense to the reader even if they don't click any links". That works for me.)This point about using your own voice is crucial:Beginner software bloggers suffer from a mass delusion that you have to write in a stiff, overly formal way for people to take you seriously [...]Just write the way you talk.With so many developers delegating their writing to AI, software blogging is becoming bland and homogenous. Readers are hungry for writing with personality.

item.title: Cristiano Ronaldo Has Lost His Damn Mind
item.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
item.content:encoded: As someone who broadly finds international breaks boring—and this current double break painfully so—I have to express gratitude to Cristiano Ronaldo for having a complete meltdown over his spot on the Portuguese national team. While his performance at the World Cup was oftentimes funny and almost always more than a little sad, this current freakout is just bizarre. OK, it’s also still pretty funny. The timeline: On Sept. 24, during the first game of this seemingly endless international break, Ronaldo started for Portugal against Wales in the first of four Nations League matches over the past fortnight. He played about as well as he did at the World Cup (so, not well at all), and was subbed off in the 67th minute. Readers with a decent memory might remember the minor hubbub over then-manager Roberto Martinez subbing Ronaldo out of the round-of-32 match against Croatia, a match Portugal would go on to win after the substitution. That controversy had nothing with what was coming, though. Three days after the Wales match, Portugal played Norway in Oslo. Ronaldo did not start that game, nor did he sub on. Portugal won, 2-1. Three days after , Ronaldo left the national team camp ahead of the Oct. 1 match against Denmark (4-2 win for Portugal), and did not show up to the final match of the break on Oct. 4 against Norway again, this time in Portugal. (You know where I’m going with this: Portugal won, 2-1.) In the middle of all that, Portuguese newspaper reported that Ronaldo hadn’t just taken his ball and gone home, but had in fact, finally, retired from the national team.

item.title: Must Every Leafy Thing Be So Freighted With Meaning? Yes, Yes It Must
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: Let's play a game. What do you expect was the outcome of this 3-on-0?Expectations are a funny thing in sports. They are as subject to the observer effect as any quantum mechanic: When a player or a team is aware of them, they may tend to play up to or exceed those expectations, or play down to them, as the case may be. Or they may be rattled and fall short. All this depends on temperament. The Maple Leafs have more observers than anyone, and their expectations are historically the least rooted in reality. Expectations and belief are two separate things, and in Toronto—at least among the 1050 caller demographic—those things are forever at war. Fans and local media that the Leafs will not achieve what is of them, even though those fans and media are the ones doing the expecting. It's a weird scene.

item.title: Blue Planet III
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: BBC Earth is returning to the ocean. 25 years after the first installment, the legendary naturalist, presenter, and centenarian David Attenborough narrates Blue Planet III. This first look video, backed by a song Hans Zimmer & Jade Thirwall, is teeming with stunning footage of sea life of all sorts.Blue Planet II is the greatest nature series that the BBC has ever produced.It is almost transcendentally good—the product of a team that, after six decades of experience, is now at the height of its powers. The Blue Planet II crew traveled to 39 countries to capture over 6,000 hours of footage. They stuck their cameras into coral crevices. They hung off speedboats to film dolphins rocketing behind them. They literally stared into the abyss—and then repeatedly entered it. The resulting episodes, each narrated by David Attenborough in his trademark velvety tones, are hour-long distillations of wonder, featuring sequences that would be breathtaking had earlier shots left you with any breath to take away.Blue Planet III will air sometime later in the year in the UK; not so sure about timelines in other locations at this point.

item.author: Giri Nathan
item.content:encoded: If you listen to a certain subset of the media—not necessarily the sports media—the state of the WNBA is dire. A generational talent is being squandered. Weak leadership has failed a league on the cusp of great opportunity. Something must be done. Once we figure out what exactly that something is, it's going to get so done. columnist Christine Brennan, who has written a book about Caitlin Clark, belongs to this subset, and has committed to viewing an entire sports league through the lens of one All-Star guard on the Indiana Fever. Clark is certainly a popular and exciting basketball player to watch, but adherence to a religiously Clarkcentric worldview can warp one's commentary over time. Eventually you come off like someone who doesn't know or care about anything else happening in the WNBA. Clark's Indiana Fever lost their first-round playoff series to the Las Vegas Aces last week, leaving Brennan to select some strained reporting angles as her book subject spun out of the postseason.Late in Game 2 of that series, Aces star forward A'ja Wilson confronted a courtside Fever fan who she felt had "disrespected" her. "If I see a man come at me, taking steps towards me and pointing at me, I don’t give a damn what you said. I don’t give a damn how you said it, the tone. That is unacceptable," Wilson told press after the game. Brennan sought comment from the WNBA and, 36 hours later, was disappointed not to have heard back. According to her, the WNBA's slow response to queries about Wilson reflects its "leadership vacuum," and a league source's bog-standard obfuscatory description of the event is somehow a "PR nightmare."

item.title: The Real Meaning of Real Extreme Temperatures
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: How hot can it get? How cold can it get? Here on earth, temperatures fluctuate wildly, but they mostly stay in the sweet spot where we can survive (Antarctica and Death Valley excluded). but in the science of measuring temperature, physicists look at the activity of atoms. There is a temperature called absolute zero, but we've never seen it and can't achieve it. We came close once, and some really weird things happened. When we take the temperature up, exploding stars are the hottest things we can think of. How can we measure them? With physics, but we don't know about any upper limit to heat, because at a certain point, measurement becomes meaningless. Beyond that, they lost me with talk about how temperature may be a loop of some kind. Space Explainer takes us through temperature extremes on earth and elsewhere, narrated by cartoon paper doll scientists on cartoon popsicle sticks, for some reason. (via Laughing Squid)

item.title: Cleta Mitchell and Tina Peters want Trump’s commerce secretary to seize voting machines
item.author: 1axbtb211adycvi3lnnbh4ao4et20n3l42bbab@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Convicted election denier Tina Peters reportedly met with President Donald Trump this week in the Oval Office to discuss plans for the midterms. Details of the meeting are scarce, but lately Peters has been pushing the president to take action to intervene in the midterms.Specifically, Peters wants Trump to pressure Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to exploit an executive order Trump signed in his first term related to protecting U.S.-made technology, by using it to seize voting machines.Peters and other election deniers are pushing the conspiracy that voting machines use parts from China, Russia and other foreign countries that make them vulnerable to hacking. On his online show, former Trump DOJ official Ed Martin said Peters discussed this conspiracy with Trump, which was recently boosted by Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. Peters has been pushing Trump to take action to control voting for the midterms and laid out a step-by-step plan for what the president can do — starting by declaring the security of voting machines a national security issue.“The president is taking it seriously,” Martin said. “If Congress won’t pass the SAVE America Act — and they won’t — then the president’s going to have to do what he’s going to do. It’s not a local issue when it’s national security. And it’s clearly national security.”It’s not a new scheme — Peters first floated this plan over the summer — but the renewed push from her and other prominent election deniers as Election Day nears is worrisome.Conservative lawyer Cleta Mitchell is pushing the same plot.“Lots of people are asking [Trump] to declare a national emergency to protect against the vulnerabilities of electronic voting systems,” Mitchell explained on social media. “It turns out that [Trump] already declared such an emergency in May 2019.”That 2019 order declared a national emergency because of the threat of foreign adversaries exploiting vulnerabilities in information and communications technology. The order banned transactions involving foreign-owned manufacturers that “present threats to the security or resiliency of critical infrastructure.”Mitchell and Peters think voting machines qualify as critical infrastructure — and that Lutnick has the power to act.

item.title: I'm tired
item.author: 1axbyk38xej0d18t2ecbxu21xrsuzaz6b7eajn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: These last few weeks before an election are always the worst. The stress and uncertainty hang over everything we do like a dense fog. We can predict a wave. We can anticipate victories and defeats. But we don't really know what will happen.And every election has surprises. Sometimes they are welcome. Other times they are soul-crushing.I have worked on campaigns that have won and campaigns that have lost. I was there when Democrats retook the House and Senate in 2006 and when, in Barack Obama's words, we took a "shellacking" in 2010. I was devastated in 2016 and found new hope in 2020.Yet this election feels different. I tell myself this is what the final weeks of an election always feel like, but I don't really believe it.The truth is that the stakes of this election, and the threats facing it, are much higher than in any election I've worked on. The President of the United States is personally trying to suppress voting rights. His administration is exploring ways to subvert the results.This means the work of lawyers — my work — has never been more critical. Yet big law firms are nowhere to be seen. Small firms like mine are carrying the load.As of this morning, my firm is litigating 83 voting and election cases in 41 states. These are not side skirmishes. These are fights in which we are on the front lines, representing clients whose right to free and fair elections is under attack.I've spent the last few weeks on the road, flying from coast to coast. This morning, I woke up at 7 a.m. to an inbox full of legal briefs ready for review. Then I gave a talk to a group of lawyers and recorded a podcast before checking my email again on the way to the airport.I'm writing this on a plane heading back to the East Coast. When I land, there will be more legal work and another speech in New York City.I remind myself that I will eventually make it back to my home outside of Washington, D.C. I’ll eventually see my dog, Blue. If I'm being entirely honest, I'm just very tired.But I keep going, because the fate of democracy is on the line. We can’t sit this fight out.I go to court because that is my duty as a lawyer. I speak out because I am a citizen.Donald Trump is trying to subvert our elections because he wants to keep power. He has built an entire movement around election denialism and voter suppression. And now democracy itself is under threat.I have said before that it is not enough for any of us — including lawyers — to simply do our jobs. We must all speak out. Democracy Docket is how I do that.

item.title: Akusmi
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: Today we’re listening to Akusmi, a French composer and multi-instrumentalist based in London. He grew up in a musical household: his parents often brought back instruments from world travel, and he started playing classical guitar at age 7. He made recordings with field recordings as a teenager, moved to London to study jazz, and composed for film and TV. His first album as Akusmi was , which came out in 2022. For last week’s Across the Horizon episode, Lara Somogyi selected the minimalist, slow-burn track “Concrescence” from it. But first we’re playing Akusmi’s latest album, , which came out in July. On it, he plays 21 instruments in concert with tabla by Sarathy Korwar, ngoni by Dudù Kouate, and more.

item.title: Quoting Jake Boggan
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I was a graph theory junkie long ago and even moved to Budapest for awhile to study among the greats. While I was there I started working on Barnette's Conjecture which came to occupy my thoughts over the next 24 years of my life, on and off as I worked in many different fields. Last summer I even thought for a few days that I had actually solved it.But it's supposedly proven here - problem 180. I don't know what to think exactly. I spent thousands of hours on that problem. I really enjoyed it. Hearing that it is solved somehow makes me sad in a far-off way, like hearing an ex-girlfriend died suddenly in a car crash. I don't know, there's probably a lot of people feeling odd emotions tonight.

item.title: Hump Day Hottie: Candice Swanepoel
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: Candice Swanepoel is a South African model who became one of the most recognizable faces in the fashion industry during the 2010s. Born in Mooi River, South Africa, in 1988, she was discovered as a teenager and quickly began building an international modeling career.Swanepoel became particularly well known through her work with Victoria’s Secret. She became a Victoria’s Secret Angel in 2010 and appeared prominently in the company’s fashion shows, catalogs, and advertising campaigns. Her work with the brand helped make her one of the most recognizable models of her generation.Beyond Victoria’s Secret, Swanepoel has worked with numerous major fashion and beauty brands and appeared in international editions of fashion magazines. Her modeling career has included both commercial campaigns and high-fashion work, allowing her to maintain a presence across different areas of the industry.She has also been recognized for her distinctive appearance and strong runway presence. Unlike models whose careers are primarily associated with one particular fashion house, Swanepoel developed a broad international profile.Outside modeling, she has been involved in business and philanthropic projects. She launched her own swimwear line, Tropic of C, which reflects her interest in fashion and beachwear.Today, Swanepoel remains a prominent figure in fashion and social media. Her career illustrates how the modeling industry changed during the rise of social media, when models increasingly became recognizable personalities and brands in their own right.

item.title: OpenAI “rogue” agent activities found on Wikimedia projects
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Given how tempting a target wikis are for rogue agent swarms, it's not a huge surprise that Wikipedia found evidence of that activity once they went looking:The Wikimedia Foundation conducted its own investigation to see whether Wikimedia websites had been similarly affected by AI agents, focusing on those operated by OpenAI. We can confirm that we have discovered some activity by these “rogue” OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms. The unauthorized bot activities included edits to our wikis, some unsuccessful attempts to exploit a public note-taking tool we host, and heavy traffic, which are described more below.They found evidence of agents editing sandbox pages, trying to use pieces of infrastructure such as Etherpad to help proxy content from elsewhere, and saw widespread crawling and "hundreds of thousands of data queries" to their Wikidata Query Service.My best guess is that most of this was a similar (or the same) swarm of agents as those that defaced that German wiki while training for research tasks.The Wikipedia sandbox wiki edits appear to have started on May 12th, and the initial test edits to the UseModWiki Sandbox page reported by that incident started on May 11th.

item.title: llm-openai-decisions 0.1a0
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: OpenAI released their new Jev-style Decisions API, as previously announced at last week's DevDay.Since I already have an llm-typesafe plugin for talking to Jev, I had GPT-6 Astra read the new OpenAI API documentation and build an plugin inspired by .Unlike Jev, the new decision model supports image input in addition to text. Both models charge for input it and not for output: OpenAI's is 10 cents per million input tokens, Jev's is 4.2 cents per million.Otherwise the API shape is similar to Jev, at least conceptually. Jev supports three question types for yes/no, choices, or scores. OpenAI Decisions supports the same three types.Install the plugin like this:llm install llm-openai-decisions Here's an example query against an image attachment:llm -m openai-decisions/gpt-6-luna \ -a https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2025/two-pelicans.jpg \ -s {: , : , : }Consult the README for full details of how to run the other types of questions.

item.title: EmbeddingGemma 2
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: For embedding models in particular, I don't think it makes sense to use a closed, proprietary, hosted-only model.Most applications of embedding models involve calculating thousands or even millions of embedding vectors and storing them for later comparison.If your model is proprietary, the vendor is likely someday going to decide to stop offering that model. They'll have a better model to replace it, but you still need to pay to re-calculate those millions of stored existing vectors.Notably, I don't want to host the model myself. I'd much rather pay a provider for a hosted model while knowing that if they ever stop hosting it I can run the open weights version myself - or find another vendor who can do that for me.

item.title: Silent Friend
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: Silent Friend is a historical drama written and directed by Hungarian filmmaker Ildikó Enyedi. Here’s the description:In the botanical garden of a medieval German university, a ginkgo tree hundreds of years old watches its human neighbors through the slip-stream of time. Among them, a young woman in 1908 attempts to break through the botany department’s masculine academic culture; an idealistic couple in 1972 performs experiments on plant communication under its branches; and a neurologist on lockdown in 2020 turns to it as he tries to push the boundaries of perception.me before seeing this movie: that is a big tree.me after seeing this movie: that is a giant, hormonal, unbearably horned up 900-year-old virgin that understands loneliness on a level that most humans could never even begin to imagine.

item.title: Who Is Behind the AI/Existential Risk Scare?
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: For years, and especially in the last month or so, we’ve been collectively inundated with an AI industry which, uncannily and bizarrely, tells us simultaneously that AI is essential, inevitable and runs a significant chance of exterminating all of us in as few as two or three years. If you’ve dipped into this debate at all, you’ve quickly come upon discussions of so-called “rationalists” or “long-termists” or supporters of “effective altruism” who are simultaneously ubiquitous among those developing AI and in the AI safety (i.e., the folks sounding the alarm) community as well. (For the sake of simplicity and brevity, I’ll refer to these folks as the “REL nexus”: rationalists, effective altruists and long-termists. This is my coinage since I don’t know a better one.) I’ve spent a fair amount of time familiarizing myself with this world and how it relates to current debates about AI. So I wanted to share my basic impressions.

item.title: The Yankees Look Meek And Flubby
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: You've been fighting it off as best you can, but the weight of the evidence is starting to hit your hips, knees and ankles in a series of small electric spasms. You've tried to explain it away as "Well, the league's weird this year," and while you're right no matter what league you're referring to, the disorientation is still there and getting worse.The Tampa Bay Rays look like they are going to win their American League Division Series, but that's not the thing that's making you nickname your persistent migraine as though it were a mischievous nephew. It's that they're making the New York Yankees look like the Los Angeles Angels, which is not just laughing at the power of branding but making a fresh mockery of a town that already has to put up with the Mets.The Rays gnaw at a game like hyperactive beavers, eschewing home runs (except for Junior Caminero) and embracing the annoying little things that modern baseball once disdained: speed, defense, and even the occasional bunt. The Yankees have struggled with stuff like catching the ball or throwing it in a useful direction, which have always been in fashion. That is how Game 2, a 5-2 Rays win, played out Monday night. The Yankees' four errors were spectacular, the second-most put up by the team in its 448 all-time postseason games, highlighted but by no means concluded by Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s comprehensive mangling of a double-play pivot on the Rays' third at-bat of the game. Had it not been for Ben Rice's two solo homers, the Yankees would have looked utterly Angelic in all the worst ways.

item.title: Defector Reads A Book Is Spooked By Some ‘Incidents Around The House’
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: The first thing I have to warn you is that if you purchase Josh Malerman's , it have a sticker on it saying it's a movie now. If that's a dealbreaker, there's no escaping it, because the movie is coming out next week and because it features one of the all-time fucked-up jump scares in a trailer. I almost can't believe that was allowed. Anyway, yes, this is the book that is based on. But several Defector staffers have previously read it and won't shut up about how good it is.The second thing to warn you about is that this book is . I am not a baby, and I read a decent amount of horror, and it's been a long, long time since I read anything that had me jumpy about leaving my bed in the middle of the night. My all-time favorites are Shirley Jackson's The Haunting of Hill House and Michael McDowell's , and I won't really hesitate to put up there with those. It's not postmodern/lit/"elevated horror," like so many of today's horror novelists seem to aspire to. This is the classic shit.Incidents Around The House is narrated by Bela, an 8-year-old girl who for some time has been visited by ... that lives in her closet, but is not confined to it. She calls this something Other Mommy, because it looks like her mother—mostly, and sometimes—and it asks her, in increasingly threatening tones, if it can go inside her heart. She tells her parents about Other Mommy, and the book is about them not trying to figure out what it is, but rather if there is any way to escape it.

item.title: Will Matthew Mayich’s Collapse Change Anything?
item.author: Lauren Theisen
item.content:encoded: The Arizona State hockey team plays their home opener on Friday, but hanging over their season, and the entire program, will be what happened to defenseman Matthew Mayich. At an outdoor, "military-style" team workout on Aug. 20, Mayich collapsed from exertional heat stroke. He's been in the hospital on life support ever since, with his family attorneys saying that he has "zero chance" of making a complete recovery.Mayich's hospitalization has shone a harsh light on both the ASU administration and the wider culture of "military-style" workouts in athletics. The guy who ran this ASU workout, Tim Ziesel, is a former Army Green Beret who pushed the players through intense exercises in high-80s heat with limited water, and he ordered extra running for those who didn't perform to his specifications. An Ontario native and 2023 St. Louis Blues draft pick who transferred to ASU from Clarkson University in upstate New York, Mayich was one of 18 new players on the roster this season and was unused to the Arizona climate, putting him more at risk for heat stroke. According to The Athletic, when Mayich collapsed to the ground, "he stayed in the sun for several minutes before four players carried him into the shade."The workout was symbolic of a philosophy that head coach Greg Powers, the only man to coach the program since it joined D-I in 2015, attempted to implement after a lackluster end to the previous season. “I hate to say the word ‘soft,’ but that’s what we were,” Powers said in May. “And it became contagious." Per The Athletic, he was known around the program for a quick temper and a willingness to insult his players. Ziesel's whole deal seems specifically engineered to appeal to a guy who's anxious about making his charges "tougher." Per ASU players, Ziesel told them during the workout that he didn't drink water during combat and that "none of [the players] were worthy of his daughter."

item.title: This Worm Has No Ifs And Many Butts
item.author: Sabrina Imbler
item.content:encoded: In the 1870s, as the research ship passed through the Philippines during its circumnavigation of the Earth, it dredged up a sponge from the gray sludge 95 fathoms (nearly 600 feet) below the surface. The scientists knew that glass sponges abounded in these waters, their bodies fragile, translucent, and curiously geometric. Sponges of this sort often house other animals, such as monogamous shrimp and various worms. So it was not exactly revelatory that the dredged-up sponge contained a worm, but the worm itself was a revelation. It had laced its body through the sponge's many passages, so much so that it might have resembled many worms. But it was just one worm whose body appeared able to branch like a tree. "The body of the annelid appears to have a furor for budding," the zoologist W. C. M'Intosh wrote in an 1879 paper describing the preserved specimen of the worm. Although M'Intosh did not comprehend this at the time, the worm had a furor for budding multiple anuses.Maria Teresa Aguado, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Göttingen in Germany, learned about branching worms as a PhD student. She had always romanticized the expedition and imagined what it was like to explore distant oceans and glimpse the life lurking at great depths. When she came across an illustration of the branching worm found off the Philippines, now called , the worm sparked a lifelong fascination. "I remember staring at it, wondering if such a creature could really exist," she wrote in an email. "How could an animal evolve such a bizarre body plan?"For more than a century, branching worms seemed extraordinarily rare, with only a single species described by science. There were some reports of branching worms found elsewhere around the world, in the Red, Tasman, and Arafuro Seas, all identified as . But in 2012, Aguado and colleagues found a second species of branching worm off of northern Australia, and then a third species off an island in Japan. Aguado began to suspect that branching worms were not so rare after all. "Perhaps there were many more species, and the old records weren’t just about one or two isolated cases, but about a widespread and diverse group," she said. She was right; in September, Aguado and colleagues published a paper in the that describes 10 probable new species of branching worms and reconstructs the evolutionary history of the strange group.

item.title: The Best Sandwich Shop in America?
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: YouTuber Rob Martinez travelled to Columbus, Ohio to tell the story of what he calls the best sandwich shop in America, Wario’s Beef and Pork. Here’s part of the transcript of owner Stephan Madias talking about the restaurant:For the longest time, especially the first two years, I was very protective of how the bread was sliced and I would not let anybody cut bread. It’s about the experience. I think about me eating the sandwich. Think about the things that happen when you get a big sandwich. You take that first bite into it. I want you to be able to, like, move this thing around. Take bites from the top, the bottom, the front, the back. And it’s held.We’re very particular, and it’s part of the reason why we don’t have the bakery cut the bread is cuz we want to sort through our things. Yes, we have volume. Yes, we have speed, but [my employees] all have the integrity that we started when we only sold five sandwiches an hour when the shop first started. That’s part of being committed to the fundamentals and being consistent.The devil’s in the details, man. You got to take the extra minute to do it. Some people like it. Some people complain about it.As a fellow sandwich overthinker, I love the ethos and the process. And man, those sandwiches do look amazing — tomato butter, homemade whiz for the cheese steaks, a chicken caesar sandwich, what is not to like?

item.title: Scrimshaw Jukebox
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I wanted to see if Claude Opus 5.5 could compose music, so I tried this:I want you to write some computer game music for me. First design simple text based format for the music and build an artifact that can play it out loud - include some example tracks in that artifactI am looking for music of the quality of the original secret of Monkey IslandIt leaned a lot harder into the Monkey Island theme than I had intended, but the results are surprisingly good.I wonder if the ability to compose competent music is similar to the 3D graphics thing - a new capability for text models that emerged in the past few months?Would need some careful experiments with other recent and not-so-recent models to confirm if this is new or if they've been able to do this for a while.

item.title: Court Ruling Hobbles Trump DOJ’s Jihad Against Elusive Threat of Noncitizen Voting
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: Judge Strikes Down Federal Ban on Noncitizen VotingIn a potentially very important ruling last week, a federal judge in south Florida concluded that the Trump administration’s effort to prosecute noncitizen voting relies on a 40-year-old federal statute that is unconstitutional.In dismissing the prosecution of a Jamaican national for illegally voting in the 2020 election, U.S. District Judge David Leibowitz (a Biden appointee) found 18 U.S.C. § 611, which outlaws voting by noncitizens in federal elections, to be a “voter qualification statute.” As such, Congress intruded on the power of the states to determine voter qualifications by passing the law outlawing noncitizen voting.“[T]he Constitution does not authorize Congress to legislate voter qualifications for federal elections,” Leibowitz ruled. “Congress has no power to say vote or vote in federal elections—that foundational power is reserved for the States, and limits Congress.”As Politico’s Kyle Cheney notes, the statute that Judge Leibowitz invalidated underpins several Trump administration noncitizen-voting prosecutions that it ramped up ahead of the midterm elections:Yet in dozens of other recent cases, announced with great fanfare by the Justice Department — often accompanied by photographs of people being arrested by Homeland Security agents — the administration is hanging its illegal voting crackdown on this very statute. Many are slated for trial in December and January.Judge Leibowitz was the first judge to ever rule on the constitutionality of the statute. To help reach his decision, Judge Leibowitz had appointed Supreme Court litigator Paul Clement as a friend of the court to advise him on the constitutionality of Congress enacting the 18 U.S.C. § 61.Given the paucity of noncitizen voting, the broader import of Judge Leibowitz’s ruling is that it undermines the Trump propaganda machine’s focus on noncitizen voting as a catch-all Big Lie that seeks to justify the federal takeover of elections, the imposition of new restrictions on voting, especially mail-in voting, and the delegitimization of elections generally.ProPublica: More than 500 U.S. citizens have been caught up in the Trump administration’s mass deportation dragnet.TPM’s Hunter Walker: An ICE challenge coin for sale on eBay is emblazoned with the slogan: “There is no hunting like the hunting of man.” It’s not clear whether the coin was officially issued by ICE.“… if Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere. Anywhere.”—Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), in a closed-door fundraiser, on the progressive movement’s “generational” chance to “break the map” of American politicsWill Dems Pull a McConnell on SCOTUS?Some Senate Democrats are threatening not to confirm any Trump nominees to the Supreme Court for the rest of his term — if they win the Senate majority next month.Jay Willis: The Conservative Takeover of SCOTUSblog Is Just What the Supreme Court Needed: The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals quickly scheduled oral arguments for Oct. 23 on whether the president can fire court-appointed U.S. attorneys — a part of his scheme to install loyalists as the top federal prosecutors in blue states. The appeal by the Trump administration comes in the case of Roger Rogoff, the court-appointed U.S. attorney in Seattle, whose firing was ruled unlawful by a federal judge from outside the district. In related news, Rogoff has agreed to staying the lower court order and to not taking office while the appeal is pending.: President Trump and his former co-defendants in the Mar-a-Lago documents case are asking the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals to delay oral arguments on whether Judge Aileen Cannon’s order permanently sealing Volume II of Special Counsel Jack Smith’s report should be overturned. In the new filing, attorneys say they need the delay because of scheduling conflicts and because they need time to confer with President Trump. The oral arguments had been rescheduled multiple times over the past several months, most recently for January, but then last week was abruptly moved up to Nov. 2, the day before the midterm elections.Trump Nixes Politico From Press PoolThe Trump White House barred Politico from boarding Air Force One for a Monday trip to Nebraska, which prevented it from serving in the presidential press pool. The White House similarly retaliated against CNN over the weekend. Along with MS Now, Politico and CNN previously went to court to overturn a Trump ban on the three outlets from accessing the White House.Trump Claims He’ll Pay for Pro-Trump AdsIn an apparent reversal, President Trump posted on social media that he and his PAC will pay for the series of four pro-Trump TV ads being aired during the stretch run of midterm election and originally paid for by the federal government.More than $10 million in taxpayer-funded ads have run since September under a $20 million DHS contract, according to the NYT.“It was unclear if the PAC would repay the U.S. government for the money already spent or just pay for ads going forward,” the WSJ reported.US Feared Drone Attack On Bombers in UKThe abrupt retreat of a dozen B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford to their home base in the U.S. came in response to intel that Iran was planning a sophisticated drone attack on the planes and their crews.On Guard On NATO’s Eastern FlankPolitico: Lithuanian PM calls for NATO plan to counter Russia’s hybrid attacksThe Global March of the Far Right: In once again elevating the Bolsonaro clan in Sunday’s election, Brazil gave the far right its most decisive victory since the country’s military dictatorship ended in 1985, Harvard’s Elizabeth McKenna writes.: Tobias Rausch of the Alternative for Germany party was elected as president of the parliament in Saxony-Anhalt, the first time since the Nazi era that a far-right politician was elected to lead a state legislature.The Televangelist Origins of Donald TrumpThe death of disgraced (is there any other kind?) televangelist Jim Bakker at age 86 lets us dip back in for a moment to the gaudy nouveau riche aesthetics of the mid-1980s out of which came endless TV preacher scandals and ultimately the public persona of Donald Trump.I used to think that the Trump aesthetic mirrored the Jim Bakkers and the Jimmy Swaggarts because they all peaked in the 1980s, which happened to coincide with the glory days of high-glam primetime soaps, which set an unfortunate standard for opulence. But I’ve come to see Trump as a secular televangelist preaching his own version of the prosperity gospel to the same marks susceptible to the same grift that powered the fleeting televangelical fortunes.Trump’s grift has been bigger and bolder, managing somehow not to have his own soul saved and or to heed a call to follow Jesus, yet being fully embraced by evangelical ministers, often literally in performative Oval Office prayer sessions. Grift knows grift.

item.title: LeBron James Is Commuting In A Fanatics Helicopter
item.author: Chris Thompson
item.content:encoded: LeBron James wasn't pretending. He really is taking daily helicopter rides from his home in New York City to the offices of his new employer, the Philadelphia 76ers. Since the start of October, the LeBron James Express (call sign N6FN) has made 18 trips between Northeast Philadelphia Airport and the Manhattan West 30th Street Heliport, plus a dozen or more shorter jaunts to and from Belmar, Teterboro, Wings Field Airport, and Philadelphia International.Because of the availability of realtime flight-tracking information, it has been possible for people on the ground to note that the helicopter shuttling James back and forth from work each day is plastered with graphics for the slapdick but ever-expanding sports and e-commerce company Fanatics. Fanatics, which now runs an events operation, a video production studio, retail sportsbooks, and an online prediction market, was founded and is run by first-class celebrity hobnobber and would-be world conqueror Michael Rubin, a native Philadelphian. Rubin was formerly a limited partner in Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment (HBSE), the sports and venue management company that owns the 76ers.Someone who works for LeBron told Front Office Sports on Monday that access to Fanatics' "corporate aviation" is part of a sponsorship deal. "It’s a feature in many of their deals with their largest athletes and we appreciate their partnership as LeBron splits his time between New York and Philadelphia," the source said. Because Rubin sold his shares of HBSE back in 2022, and because James signed his present sponsorship deal with Fanatics back in 2024, this particular benefit of playing for the 76ers is not considered circumvention of the salary cap. It is merely a benefit of being in business with Fanatics while working in Philadelphia, for the favorite team of a man who at one time or another has owned some or all of both enterprises.

item.title: No biggie, it’s just our shithole president, inviting Iran to ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: “And again, remember. With the war, it’s just artificial. It’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay. for keeping the world safe. For keeping our country safe. They could take out a city. Let ’em take— let it— let ’em take out Los Angeles. Let ’em take our San Diego. That’s— this is a very small price to pay.”Wait a minute — did this depraved shithead just give Iran permission to nuke a couple of our cities? Did he actually call such an act ‘a very small price to pay’?Is Preznit Fuckwit … ? Is he serious? Is he so demented that he has no idea what he’s actually saying? Does it even matter why Donny said what he said? Dude is clearly unfit for office, and growing worse by the day.Where are you, worthless scribblers of the corporate-controlled press?Imagine that Sleepy Joe Biden’s autopen had blundered its way into an unwinnable war, and then invited our adversary to nuke the shit out of us. The press would have had a field day, falling all the fuck over themselves in a mad dash to file their stories.Jake Tapper would have orgasmed on the spot.Where are the calls for Donny to resign?Remember Joe Biden’s last year in office? The press had their knives out. Every time Joe stumbled over a word, or took too long to reply to a question, every newspaper in the land would shit out editorial after editorial, calling Biden icky and old and smelly, and demanding that he resign immediately, Where are you now, O Glorious Editorial Writers? Donny is in fact icky and old — and he probably smells like shit. Have you seen one call for Dear Leader to step down, ? I haven’t. Why the fuck not?Shouldn’t Donny calling for the deaths of millions of Americans be a more important story than Joe Biden taking three seconds to remember a diplomat’s name? In any sane world, it would be. Let’s fucking go, media. Do your goddamned jobs.“You need to be a student at the top of your class at MIT to turn on a lawnmower nowadays, you know? But I got rid of all that stuff. Now you can have a LAWNMOWER. Boom!!”What is this fucking idiot — this pampered fool — who has never done a day’s labor in his life, imagine he’s done to improve? What did he?What is he hallucinating about? Last summer, I bought a new lawnmower. It was the same as every lawnmower I’ve had since the 1960s. You pull the string and it goes vroom-vroom. Hey Jake Tapper, maybe you can explain it to me. What exactly has Donny done to Make Lawnmowers Great Again?Why is the crowd clapping like trained seals at Dear Leader’s fever-swamp bullshit? My god, they’re just as brain dead as he is.Again, Donny has been getting away with this shit for literal years, nattering on and on about stoves that don’t light, or toilets you have to flush a million times. Where are the worthless scribblers?“It’ll end very quickly and prices are gonna come down very sharply. You might say, ‘please, please, sir, it’s going down too fast!’ You watch. You watch what’s going to happen in a very short period of time.”Ohhhhh, okay. This unwinnable don’t-you-dare-call-it-a-war on Iran — the one that was only supposed to last one day; the one that Donny has claimed we’ve already won twenty times or more — now, it’s going to end very quickly. Any day now, just you wait and see — and then prices will plummet, and big, strong cultists, the afternoon sun rippling off their massive biceps, blinded by the uncontrollable tears of joy coursing down their ruddy cheeks, grateful for cheap gas like few thought possible, and the easy-to-start lawnmowers like no one’s ever seen before, and the radioactive craters where Los Angeles and San Diego used to be — they will all come up to Dear Leader and go ‘sir! sir! we can’t stand it any more! it’s going down too fast! Sir!”And then, pigs will start flying out of my ass. Donny never stops promising us that there’s going to be so much wining, we’re going to get tired of all the winning. Fuck that noise. I’m still waiting for the winning to start.Wouldn’t you love it if our press would spend even ten minutes honestly reporting on any of this shit?Top California officials denounce President Trump after he Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San DiegoDear Leader to say what he said. How helpful of you to point that out, CNN. I can’t wait for CNN’s report that San Diego to be a smoking ruin.﻿First Thing: ‘Deranged’ and ‘dangerous’ Trump calls for Iran to strike US cities amid historic ratings lowThat’s more like it. Are you paying attention, US press?It’s time for a palate cleanse. Let’s watch in awe as Davram Stiefler of the Good Liars tries and fails to get a gang of cultists to answer the age-old question, Davram Stiefler: “Is everyone worried about socialism?” MAGA: “Oh, 100%. It never works” Stiefler: “For the viewers, what is socialism?” MAGA: “Socialism is pretty much, I mean, it’s control of everything, I mean, they want control and there’s no… uhm… I don’t even… how to explain it, but… you have no control at all. I mean it’s just, it’s their way or the highway” Stiefler: “But as an economic form of governance, what is it?” I can’t even with these dumbfucks. The definition of socialism as an economic form of governance is . Thanks a lot, Brainiac. You’ve really done us a solid with that simple explanation.Here’s your hero of the day: it’s The Man Who Convicts War Criminals In The Hague.Jack Smith was spotted at an outdoor music festival this past weekend, wearing a ‘No Kings’ tee-shirt.Maybe Donny should invite Iran to nuke Jack Smith. Y’know, kill two birds with one stone.Hey, let’s do some Daily Claudia.Here we have a trio of selfies that I pulled off of Ms Spouse’s phone, from July 15, 2023. Ms Spouse sure did love her hats. She had dozens. I think I ended up gifting this one to bff Kathy.Have a great Tuesday, everyone. Remember, the worst thing about socialism is that it’s socialism. here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: White Sox Touched By God, Or Perhaps Merely Joyful Exuberance
item.author: Kathryn Xu
item.content:encoded: At the start of Game 2 of their ALDS matchup Monday, Chicago White Sox starter-turned-reliever-turned-opener Anthony Kay faced the Cleveland Guardians offense and posed a powerful question. What would be more powerful: a papal blessing or Guardiansball, an offensive strategy best defined by the example phrase of "Steven Kwan infield single"? Well, immediately after the bottom of the first inning, Guardiansball was winning out.Kwan himself led off affairs by hitting a ground ball that trickled its way out of the infield for a single. José Ramírez walked. Chase DeLauter moved both runners into scoring position with another ground ball. Kay was pulled for White Sox reliever-stayed-reliever Sean Newcomb, who immediately went down 2-0 in the count to Jo Adell, before intentionally walking him. Nathaniel Lowe came up to bat and then booped a high chop that bounced right to Newcomb. The Guardians then implemented the second core piece of their strategy, "opposing team forgets how to place defense." Newcomb whipped the ball way off mark for a throwing error, allowing two runs to score. He went on to strike out the next two batters. And so the fourth-worst slugging team in baseball this year ended the first inning with a two-run lead, despite failing to elevate the ball even once.It was the first time in the White Sox's 2026 playoff run that the team started a game trailing and, permitting me to take even more indulgence in small playoff sample sizes, the first runs scored in by the Guardians in the series. The circumstances were in place for the White Sox's blessed playoff run to stall out, with the Guardians at home, their starter Gavin Williams well-rested and regularly hitting triple digits on the radar gun, and the White Sox's strategy of generously deploying openers looking suspiciously close to a cheap knock-off version of the Dodgers' "Oops, all starting pitchers!" approach to bullpen construction.

item.title: The Invisible Servants of The Elms
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: It's hard to believe, but this 60,000 square foot mansion is sometimes referred to as a summer cottage. This is The Elms in Newport, Rhode Island, built as a summer getaway for Edward Julius Berwind. Sure, it's big, but to guests it was a lot smaller on the inside than the outside. They wouldn't even notice that, because of the sheer size and opulence of the home. The rest of the house was hidden, because that's where the huge staff lived and worked. The interior was designed so that you never saw the work going on; the cleaning, cooking, and serving just happened as if by magic.While the servants' quarters and work spaces are plain compared to the family and guest spaces at The Elms, they still look quite fancy to the modern eye. Architectural Digest shows us many of the engineering tricks and illusions that kept the dirty work behind genteel living hidden in The Elms.

item.title: Sign Of The Times … Texas Edition
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: It’s surprising to see Donald Trump campaigning in Texas a month before a midterm election, as he will this week. Far more surprising to see him snubbed by the incumbent Republican governor who until as recently as a month ago appeared to be in an all but nominal reelection campaign against state Rep. Gina Hinojosa. Houston Chronicle reporter Ben Wermund caught up with Greg Abbott who told Wermund he wouldn’t be able to show up because of “other campaign events already planned.” Said Abbott: “Whenever he does show up, it leads to excitement with the base. He does a good job with getting the base organized and turning out.”He “does a good job.” lol …While I am certainly not predicting Abbott’s defeat, recent polls have shown a genuinely competitive race. Fox and Siena polls both take in the last week of September showed at Abbott +5 (Fox) or Hinojosa +4 (NYT/Siena). A Marist poll a week earlier showed Hinojosa +3. A few lesser known or GOP sponsored polls have leaned more toward Abbott. An additional concern for Abbott is that Ken Paxton seems to be running genuinely behind. So Abbott could also pick up some some of the downdraft from that race.

item.title: "Take a look at California": Trump's roadmap for attacking the midterms
item.author: 1axcfkrug2ymtkj60fzi5wuzhttvq41xmj44u7@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: On Monday afternoon, a reporter asked Donald Trump why, if he was so worried about fraud, he was telling his supporters to vote by mail. Trump said he had "no choice because a lot of people want to vote by mail."He then launched into his usual baseless allegations of fraud. Pressed to say where this fraud had taken place, he told reporters to "start off by taking a look at California."With the midterms less than a month away, we have become sadly accustomed to Trump's false attacks on free and fair elections. But his focus on California is more than routine. It is both a decade-long fixation and a roadmap for his plans in 2026.Weeks after winning in 2016, Trump blamed "serious voter fraud" in California for his loss of the popular vote by nearly 3 million votes. He has repeated the charge in every election cycle since.In 2019, he claimed California had "admitted to a million [illegal] votes" in a court settlement. It hadn't. In 2020, his false claims about California's mail ballots earned him Twitter's first-ever fact-check label on one of his posts. In 2024, he told Dr. Phil that "if Jesus Christ came down and was the vote counter, I would win California."This year, the rhetoric has escalated into action. Trump has called California "one of the most dishonest states" and told Fox News that its "mail-in votes are a fraud."On June 5, three days after the state's primary, Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, announced that his office was conducting "multiple election fraud investigations." Weeks later, Trump bragged that he had personally phoned the "U.S. attorney in California" with a request: "Do me a favor. Take a look."Around the same time, Jay Clayton, then the U.S. attorney in Manhattan, went on CNBC to question California's voting rules, claiming they created "an opportunity for fraud." Days later, Trump nominated him to be director of national intelligence.Trump's obsession with California isn't just about the fact that he has repeatedly lost the state in landslides, or that it is reliably controlled by Democrats. It's that he sees California as the biggest obstacle to stopping a Democratic wave in November.

item.title: Missing Link
item.author: Ernie Smith
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.content:encoded: Some spare thoughts about Link, a newspaper that turned 20 years old today—but more or less changed my life. It's been 18 years, but I still miss that job.As I’ve written in the past, I look longingly at the era of the free daily newspaper. It was an era that represented much of my traditional newspaper career, and it’s one that has been more or less forgotten about by mainstream journalism.But I had the chance to work at three of them, one of which was among the largest of its kind in the country, the . I loved that paper, though I admit that when I think back to my time in newspapers, I think about above everything else., a publication of the that began its life 20 years ago today, started with a provocative idea: What if you could take a 30-column-inch story and condense it into a 3-column-inch story? You could present the information in a new way, leaning on alternative story forms; you could make room for more visuals. And you could inform someone who might not have time for a long-form newspaper in a matter of minutes.I think fondly of this paper for a number of reasons. To keep in the spirit of the alt-story-form in which it worked: The format of the newspaper was always a bit like a puzzle to me. We essentially were building a magazine from scratch five days a week, sometimes producing ambitious pages without even knowing what would be on the front page that day. Though I was a designer, this was the first real experience I got with editing copy, learning the process of taking a story down to the studs and still making it feel dynamic and informative. It taught me a lot about brevity and telling a story through its elements, not just through prose. It was a strange newsroom by the time it ended; four designers, six copy editors, a web guy, a single reporter, and the editor-in-chief. In most newsrooms, this order would be flipped entirely. But this made room for a ton of ideas, as we took the best of the and presented it to people who would never pick up a copy of the otherwise. (What was also great was that some folks in the main newsroom actually made time for us nerds.) I had never lived in a community quite like Norfolk, which was small enough to be accessible but large enough that there was always something going on. In terms of real life, it was probably the most social I’ve ever felt living somewhere. I’m actually still in touch with some of the folks I met during this era, both in the newsroom and outside of it. After this paper shut down, it inspired me to start a blogging career that was driven by this format. I’ve more or less have been doing it ever since, though I write a lot more than I did in 2006.While this little newspaper had lots of little strengths, there were some weaknesses with the format that perhaps are more obvious from a healthy distance. Most free daily newspapers were intended for commuter-friendly towns, generally to be read on the train or bus. Hampton Roads, alas, is infamously a car-centric community with a number of bridge-tunnels connecting its various parts. Despite being a factor in its creation, the region only got its first light rail system three years Link ended, and that system has yet to get out of Norfolk to any of the numerous other cities in the region.The other factor, and not an uncommon one with papers of its type: Its internet presence was more or less anemic. (Yes, given the name, somewhat ironic.) Unlike so many newspapers of its era, it didn’t have much of a website, in part out of concern that it would directly compete with the main publication, and in part because the paper effectively was a reformatting of long-form newspaper content in an inventive way.It ended in the same sad way so many other things ended: As news of the 2008 recession was breaking, we found out layoffs were happening at the , and it was strongly hinted that would be on the chopping block. But it did not shut down right away, but with a two-month delay, with the paper ending just before Christmas, 2008. Unlike Lehman Brothers, we had a proper chance to say a very long goodbye to this job we all loved. (A sign that there might have been some regrets about this shift: About six months after the paper shut down, when I was merely visiting Norfolk, I ran into the business executive in charge of the ’s publishing businesses at a coffee shop, and, seemingly embarrassed to be running into a guy he laid off not that long ago, he sheepishly suggested that he would try to bring this paper back. I’m probably safe to assume it’s not happening at this point.)Two decades later, I still find myself looking back at this era, with this job that paid more in the form of freedom than it did money, and thinking I had it all figured out. At least some of the glass is rose-tinted, I will admit. But ultimately, set me up for a different kind of success after the 27-month experience of a great job ended. I ended up getting my gig at and moving to D.C., where I immediately met my future wife, and found myself becoming a blogger of modest note. I would sometimes get yelled at for showing up to the paper too early to work, not because I was trying to score overtime, but because I was excited by the work. I eventually put that energy into the digital realm instead.At this point, I’m pretty much a fully digital creature. But it’s hard to get the ink stains off my fingers all these years later, and while I had the bug before I worked at , it was where it really stuck for me. I still integrate alt-story-form into my various projects, and if I ever find a pocket of time to build it, I still own the domain to the former website, as well as a newspaper box that currently sits in my living room.Over the past few years, an art collective driven by fans of has been periodically publishing new versions of the newspaper, independently of . I’m probably not doing any of that. While I don’t have a printing press at my disposal, I do have a bunch of old issues, some PDFs, and a brain full of memories. Oh, and the box. And the domain.
